It brings data discovery, consent and protection along with security intelligence in an on-premise appliance, keeping sensitive processing within your infrastructure Local processing Deploy inside your infrastructure, with options for isolated environments Privacy controls Discover sensitive data, manage consent and protect what you share Security intelligence Connect identity, voice and media signals to investigate threats Evidence built in Keep control activity and supporting evidence ready for review Discuss your deployment The doctrine Detected Enforced Evidenced One operating layer: security teams connect signals into explainable evidence, while privacy teams manage consent, data requests and their compliance record Core platform architecture Every signal, one platform Fifteen engines in, one verdict out, with the working behind it › FaceOff Platform · Engine online › Deepfake & manipulated media detection · Image, video, audio › Identity verification · Liveness, face match, document checks › Voice intelligence · Synthetic speech & caller fraud flagged › Digital threat monitoring · Phishing, impersonation, brand abuse › Physical-world risk · Weapons, intrusion & anomaly alerts › Data discovery · Sensitive data mapped across every system › Consent & cookie management · 1,200+ regulations, one console › DSAR automation · Requests fulfilled with an audit trail › AI governance · Model inventory, lineage & regime assessment › Evidence built in · Every decision recorded, append-only › On-premise ready · Runs inside your perimeter From FaceOff Technologies TRUST FACTOR TRUST FACTOR The multimodal intelligence engine behind every FaceOff verdict Vision / Audio / Physiology The platform Three pillars. Prompt & file inspection Sanitized & routed Warned or blocked Key benefits What changes once it is running 01 Fraud stopped before it completes Impersonation is caught at onboarding, in the call and at the payment, while the transaction can still be refused, not in the reconciliation that follows it 02 Regulatory exposure reduced The DPDP Act carries up to ₹250 Cr for a failure of reasonable security safeguards, assessed per instance. Controls that run continuously are what stands between you and that number 03 Investigations that hold up Forensic reports, per-decision detection chains and provenance tiers on every output mean a finding can be defended to a board, a regulator or a court 04 One programme, many regulators One catalogue, one control library and one assessment engine serve every regime you are in scope for, instead of a separate project each time a jurisdiction moves Why choose FaceOff Trust you can verify Compliance that never sleeps Why FaceOff Read the DPDP brief Continuous 100% Append only audit trail Unified 1 Engine Security and privacy together 01 What does the platform do for data security It detects deepfakes, manipulated media, synthetic voices, identity fraud and digital threats across image, video, audio and documents, then connects those signals into one investigation so teams see the whole picture instead of one alert 02 What does the platform do for data privacy Consent, cookies, data discovery, PIA and DPIA assessments, DSARs and audit evidence run from one privacy graph, so every record, control and request shares a single source of truth across your organisation 03 How does it help with DPDP and global regulations An AI copilot reads more than 1,200 regulations including India DPDP, GDPR, CCPA and the EU AI Act against your own controls and evidence, and answers with citations so compliance teams always know the practical next step 04 How is evidence kept for audits and investigations Every security verdict keeps its supporting observations and every privacy action keeps its evidence timeline in an append only record, so a regulator, a board or an investigator can see exactly how a decision was reached 05 Can it run inside our own infrastructure Yes, deploy as managed cloud, private cloud, on premise, edge or fully air gapped, including the in a Box appliance, so sensitive media, personal data and prompts never have to leave your perimeter 06 Why one platform instead of separate security and privacy tools One engine, the Trust Factor, scores media, identity, voice, consent and data risk together, which removes duplicate tooling, closes the gaps between teams and gives leadership one trusted answer instead of five dashboards CERTIFIED · ATTESTED · COMPLIANT Prove what your teams can trust Security is more than a score Privacy is a system content.text: AI Governance | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / AI Governance AI Governance · Module 09 AI Governance DPDP made algorithmic accountability a statutory duty, not a policy aspiration. Sec. 10(2)(c)(iii) obliges a Significant Data Fiduciary to perform due diligence on algorithmic software that may risk the rights of Data Principals — which means knowing what models you run, on what data, with what oversight. Book a DPDP walkthrough All AI Governance Platform capabilities Model register with owners EU AI Act + DPDP assessment Decision-level explainability Primary DPDP sections Sec. 10(2)(c)(iii) Regimes assessed from one description 9 Regimes assessed from one description Reasoning layers exposed per decision 5 Reasoning layers exposed per decision Figures illustrative. How it works AI Governance, end to end Algorithmic due diligence becomes a standing record rather than a scramble: which models touch personal data, how each was assessed, and who signed off the residual risk 01 Register Every model in production, with owner, purpose and training-data provenance 02 Classify EU AI Act risk tier and DPDP Sec. 10 applicability 03 Assess Bias and fairness testing, human-oversight design documented 04 Explain Per-decision detection chain: which layers agreed, which dismissed 05 Evidence Residual risk signed off, findings tracked to closure Sec. 10(2)(c)(iii): due diligence of algorithmic software that may risk the rights of Data Principals. Capability What AI Governance does Model inventory & lineage A register of every model in production, the personal data it was trained on, the purpose it serves and the decisions it influences. Models registered with owner and purpose Training-data provenance recorded Lineage from data source to decision Shadow and third-party models surfaced Assessment against nine regimes The same assessment engine that runs DPIAs covers the EU AI Act, so one description of a system produces the output each regulator expects. EU AI Act risk classification DPDP Sec. 10 algorithmic due diligence Bias and fairness testing recorded Human-oversight design documented Explainability & consensus Detection and classification decisions expose which layer produced them and which dismissed them, so a finding can be defended rather than merely reported. Per-decision detection chain retained Layer-level agreement, not a black box False-positive auditing built in Provenance tiers on every output Outcome Algorithmic due diligence becomes a standing record rather than a scramble — you can show which models touch personal data, how each was assessed, and who signed off the residual risk. DPDP alignment AI Governance — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 10(2)(c)(iii) Undertake such other measures as prescribed, including due diligence of algorithmic software that may risk the rights of Data Principals. Algorithmic due diligence runs as a dedicated assessment type covering model purpose, training-data provenance, bias testing and human oversight, tracked per model rather than per programme. Sec. 10(2)(c)(i) A Significant Data Fiduciary must undertake periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments. Models are assessed on the same cadence and in the same engine as processing activities, so an AI system is never assessed outside the privacy programme that governs its data. Sec. 8(3) Ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency of personal data where it is used to make a decision affecting the Principal. Model lineage ties each decision back to the attributes and copies that fed it, so accuracy obligations reach the inputs of automated decisions rather than stopping at the system of record. Sec. 11 The Principal may obtain a summary of the processing activities performed on their personal data. Automated processing is disclosed as a named activity with its purpose and its model, rather than being hidden inside a system description. Exposure avoided Sec. 10 duties carry up to ₹150 Cr, and SDF status is notified by the Central Government by class — an enterprise can acquire algorithmic due-diligence obligations without changing a line of its own code. Book a readiness walkthrough See the platform Act DPDP Act, 2023 Obligations 18 mapped to products Max penalty ₹250 Cr, per instance Applies to Every Data Fiduciary Maximum penalty for failing to take reasonable security safeguards ₹250 Cr Maximum penalty for failing to take reasonable security safeguards For failing to intimate a breach — and separately for children's-data failures ₹200 Cr For failing to intimate a breach — and separately for children's-data failures For a Significant Data Fiduciary that misses its Sec. 10 obligations ₹150 Cr For a Significant Data Fiduciary that misses its Sec. 10 obligations Schedule penalties are assessed per instance. The Act Obligation by obligation The duties that attach to every Data Fiduciary, and the additional ones that attach once the Central Government notifies you as Significant. Sec. 4 & 7 Lawful grounds Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose, with consent or for a listed legitimate use. Sec. 5 Notice Itemised notice: what data, what purpose, how to exercise rights, how to complain to the Board — in English or any Eighth Schedule language. Sec. 6 Consent Free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, by clear affirmative action. Withdrawal as easy as giving. Sec. 8 Fiduciary duties Accuracy, technical and organisational measures, reasonable security safeguards, erasure on withdrawal, published DPO contact — and liability for processors. Sec. 9 Children Verifiable parental or guardian consent; no tracking or behavioural advertising directed at children. Sec. 10 Significant Data Fiduciary DPO based in India, independent data auditor, periodic DPIA and audit, algorithmic due diligence. Sec. 11–14 Principal rights Access summary, correction and erasure, grievance redressal, nomination. Sec. 16 Cross-border Transfer permitted except to countries restricted by the Central Government by notification. catalogue. Masking and breach detection come second because Sec. 8(5) and 8(6) carry ₹250 Cr and ₹200 Cr — the largest exposure buys down earliest. Consent follows because it is the longest change-management effort and depends on knowing what is actually collected. Rights and audit come last because they consume what the first three phases built. Enforcement timeline The Rules are notified. The deadline is 13 May 2027 The 2023 Act set the duties; the Rules notified on 13 November 2025 made them operative. Enterprise programmes typically need 9 to 12 months from gap assessment to audit readiness. 13 Nov 2025 DPDP Rules notified The Rules were notified, turning the 2023 Act into operative obligations with detail on notice, consent, security safeguards and breach reporting. From Nov 2025 Data Protection Board stands up The Board becomes operational and the complaint mechanism goes live, so a Data Principal has somewhere to take a grievance. ~Nov 2026 Consent Manager registration opens Consent Managers — registered intermediaries with a minimum net worth of ₹2 crore — can register with the Board. Fiduciaries that intend to interoperate need their consent artefacts in the right shape before this. 13 May 2027 Full compliance required Every organisation processing digital personal data in India must be fully compliant. Enterprise programmes typically run 9–12 months from gap assessment to audit readiness, so the window to start is now. Hard deadline Dates reflect the Rules as notified on 13 November 2025. Verify against the official notification before relying on them contractually. Questions DPDP, answered The questions that come up in every readiness conversation. What is the DPDP Act, 2023? The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is India's data protection law. It governs how organisations — Data Fiduciaries — may process the digital personal data of individuals, called Data Principals. It requires a lawful purpose, itemised notice, specific and informed consent, security safeguards, breach intimation, and a defined set of rights including access, correction, erasure and grievance redressal. When is the DPDP compliance deadline? The DPDP Rules were notified on 13 November 2025, and full compliance is required by 13 May 2027. The Data Protection Board and its complaint mechanism are already operational, and Consent Manager registration is expected to open around November 2026. Most enterprise programmes take 9 to 12 months from gap assessment to audit readiness. What are the penalties under the DPDP Act? The Schedule sets penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards, up to ₹200 crore for failing to intimate a personal data breach, up to ₹200 crore for children's-data failures, up to ₹150 crore for a Significant Data Fiduciary that misses its Section 10 duties, and up to ₹50 crore for other contraventions. Penalties are assessed per instance. Who is a Significant Data Fiduciary? The Central Government may notify any Data Fiduciary, or a class of them, as Significant based on the volume and sensitivity of the data processed and the risk to Data Principals. An SDF must appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India who is answerable to the board, appoint an independent data auditor, and carry out periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments, audits and due diligence of algorithmic software. An enterprise can become an SDF without changing anything it does. What is a Consent Manager under the DPDP Act? A Consent Manager is a registered intermediary that gives a Data Principal a single accessible, transparent and interoperable point to give, review and withdraw consent across multiple Data Fiduciaries. Registration is with the Data Protection Board and carries a minimum net-worth requirement. It is distinct from a Consent Management Platform, which is the software an organisation runs internally to capture and enforce consent. Does the DPDP Act require consent for cookies? The Act requires consent by clear affirmative action before processing begins. In practice that means non-essential cookies and trackers must not fire until the visitor has opted in — prior blocking — with rejection as easy as acceptance and no pre-ticked boxes. A tag that fires before the affirmative action is unlawful processing from the first pageview, and no consent receipt recorded afterwards can retrofit it. How long do we have to respond to a DSAR? The Act gives Data Principals rights of access, correction, completion, updating, erasure, grievance redressal and nomination, and requires a response within the prescribed period. Meeting that clock at volume depends on being able to locate every store holding a given individual's data, which is why a live data catalogue is a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have. How does DPDP compare to GDPR? Both require a lawful basis, notice, security safeguards, breach reporting and individual rights, so a mature GDPR programme covers much of the ground. DPDP differs in important ways: consent is the primary basis with a narrower set of legitimate uses, notice must be available in English or any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages, verifiable parental consent is required for children with a ban on behavioural advertising directed at them, and the Consent Manager is a registered intermediary with no direct GDPR equivalent. What the engine measures No single signal is reliable on its own. Cross-modal agreement is what separates a real recording from a convincing synthetic one. Deepfake Detection Facial structure, expression, and motion are analysed over time alongside texture, boundary, reflection, and lighting cues to identify signs of manipulated or synthetic video. Detail → Facial Emotion Recognition Facial muscle movement and visible expression patterns are tracked over time to identify emotional cues that may not be clear from a single still frame. Detail → Eye Tracking Analysis Gaze behaviour, fixation, and pupil response are analysed as visible signals of emotional state, with changes in eye movement and gaze patterns considered over time. Detail → Posture & Behaviour Body position and movement patterns are analysed over time to identify physical cues associated with the emotional states expressed through posture and movement. Detail → Heart Rate from Video Pulse estimated from facial colour signal, revealing arousal that expression alone conceals. Detail → Speech Sentiment Vocal pattern, rhythm, and prosody decoded into sentiment independent of what was said. Detail → Audio Tone Sentiment Pitch, energy, and timbre analysed for the emotional colour underneath the words. Detail → Oxygen Saturation SpO2 estimated from video, adding a physiological channel that is hard to fake convincingly. It is an engineering one. Privacy control plane Policy active Data inventory Customer records Classified Payment data Classified Support history Classified Purpose controls Consent by purpose Regional policy Retention rules Enforced everywhere Evidence log 0 1 Consent recorded 0 2 Access limited 0 3 Audit trail sealed Proof available on demand Verified Products Eight on one fabric DPDP obligations 18 owned, no gap column Regimes DPDP · GDPR · CCPA · LGPD · PIPEDA Readiness Phased over 26 weeks OVERVIEW Privacy that operates as designed Know where every trace of personal data lives. Capture consent that actually holds. Enforce it across every system and prove it on demand. Products on one shared privacy fabric 8 Products on one shared privacy fabric DPDP obligations owned, with no gap column 18 DPDP obligations owned, with no gap column Regimes on one control library — DPDP, GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, LGPD, PIPEDA 5 Regimes on one control library — DPDP, GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, LGPD, PIPEDA What breaks today Consent sits in a banner tool. Personal data sits in forty systems Nothing reconciles the two, so consent is unenforceable the moment it is given. Nobody can answer “where is this person's data?” without a manual hunt — which does not fit inside a statutory clock. One catalogue One catalogue of personal data, one consent record of truth, one policy engine, one audit trail. Eight products, one fabric A rights request, an audit and a breach notification all resolve against the same records rather than three reconstructions. Regulation as configuration Each regime is expressed as configuration over a shared control library. DPDP is a mapping, not a rebuild. The platform Eight products. One privacy fabric Shared beneath every product: data catalogue, identity resolution, policy engine, AI classification and an immutable evidence trail. T + 0s Withdrawal captured Consent Management records the withdrawal against the specific purpose and stamps it. Click-parity is enforced against the original give-flow. Consent Management T + 1s Purpose revoked The policy engine revokes the purpose and fans the event out to every processor that inherited that consent. Privacy Program Governance T + 2s Stores located Discovery returns every store holding that Principal's data; erasure executes against the list. It works during onboarding, during an interview, and at the moment a payment is approved, without asking the customer to stop and prove themselves again. One session · four lanes · a step-up only on drift One session · start to now Sign-in Now Typing rhythm Pointer path Device posture Interaction cadence Drift Confidence A step-up is requested where the band drifts, and nowhere else. The rest of the session is never interrupted. A password proves somebody knew a secret. A one time code proves somebody held a phone. Neither proves that the person on the other side is who your records say, that they are really there, or that they meant to do what they just did. BehaviorID answers those questions instead. It confirms that a live person is present rather than a photograph or a recording, that they are the person who enrolled, and that they are acting of their own accord. Because the check reads what is already happening, the customer is not asked to stop and complete an extra step. Organisations use it at the points where being wrong is expensive. Opening an account for someone who does not exist. Interviewing a candidate who is not the person who applied. Releasing a payment that the account holder never authorised. In each case the record needs to show not only that a credential was used, but that a person stood behind it. Products across behavioural identity and payments 3 Products across behavioural identity and payments Confirmed present rather than photographed or recorded Live person Confirmed present rather than photographed or recorded The check reads the interaction already taking place No extra step The check reads the interaction already taking place In this category 3 products. One question , asked at three moments Identity is worth confirming when an account is opened, when someone is interviewed, and when money moves. There is a product for each of those moments, and each returns an answer a reviewer can act on. BehaviorBioAuth (Onboarding) Behavioral biometric identity verification. They open an account, answer questions, or approve a payment exactly as they would have anyway. Onboarding A new account or application Interview A conversation on the record Payment approval The moment money moves As it happens One question Is a real person behind this Present now, not a photograph or a recording The person who enrolled, not a lookalike Acting willingly, not under pressure Consistent with how they behaved before The person is never asked to prove it twice The check reads the interaction that was already happening, so nothing is added to the customer's journey. Proceed, or pause A clear outcome the system can act on A record of why For a reviewer, an auditor or a case file 01 Enrol once The person is registered a single time, at a moment when their identity is already being established. Everything afterwards is checked against that first registration. 02 Carry on as normal When they next open an account, sit an interview or approve a payment, they do it in the ordinary way. Nothing asks them to pause, repeat a phrase or complete a puzzle. 03 The check runs alongside While that is happening, the interaction is assessed for whether a live person is present, whether they match the person who enrolled, and whether they appear to be acting freely. 04 A decision, with its reasons A clear outcome comes back so the system can proceed, pause or ask for a second check. The reasons behind it are kept, so a reviewer can see later why the call was made. Use cases Where organisations put it to work Three moments, one question. These are the situations teams bring to the category most often. Banking and financial services Confirm that a new account is being opened by a real person rather than an invented identity, and that a payment is being approved by the account holder rather than by someone who has taken over the session. Payments and digital wallets Let customers approve a payment by presenting themselves rather than by recalling a password or waiting for a code. The approval is tied to the person and to that transaction. Recruitment and remote hiring Establish that the candidate being interviewed is the person who applied, and keep a record of the session that a hiring panel can review afterwards. Insurance Verify the claimant during a remote interview, and keep a reviewable record of the conversation for the file rather than relying on the assessor's recollection. Government and public services Confirm a real applicant is present when a benefit, licence or entitlement is claimed remotely, without requiring a visit to a counter. Enterprise access and approvals Protect the approvals that matter, such as releasing funds or granting elevated access, by confirming the approver is present and acting willingly. FAQ What people ask about BehaviorID Answered the way a fraud lead, a hiring manager or a compliance officer asks them. What is BehaviorID? − BehaviorID is FaceOff's suite for confirming that a real, enrolled person is present and acting willingly. It is used when an account is opened, when someone is interviewed, and when a payment is approved. Rather than asking the person to prove themselves with a password or a code, it reads the interaction that is already taking place and reports whether a genuine person stands behind it. How is this different from a password or a one time code? + A password proves somebody knew a secret and a one time code proves somebody held a phone. Neither proves that the person is real, that they are the account holder, or that they meant to approve what they just approved. BehaviorID answers those questions instead, which is why it holds up in situations where credentials have been stolen, shared or handed over under pressure. Does the customer have to do anything extra? + No. The check reads the interaction that was already happening, so the person opens their account, answers the interview questions or approves the payment exactly as they would have done anyway. There is no additional step, no phrase to repeat and no puzzle to complete, which is the point: a check people have to cooperate with is a check people avoid. Can it tell whether someone is being coerced? + Assessing whether a person appears to be acting willingly is part of what BehaviorID looks for, which matters most at the moment a payment is approved. It is reported as an assessment for a person to weigh rather than as a certainty, and like every result it arrives with the reasons behind it so a reviewer can judge it rather than accept it. What happens to the biometric information involved? + BehaviorID is designed so that confirming a person does not leave an organisation holding a new central collection of faces and voices. Where the approval happens on a customer's own device, the assessment is designed to complete there rather than sending the material elsewhere. Analysis can also be run inside an organisation's own environment where the material is sensitive or must not leave a jurisdiction. Who uses BehaviorID? + BehaviorID is used by banks and payment providers confirming account holders and approvals, insurers verifying claimants during remote interviews, employers establishing that the candidate interviewed is the person who applied, and public bodies confirming applicants who never visit a counter. What these teams share is that a credential alone is no longer enough evidence that a person was there. Is a result ever wrong? + BehaviorID produces an evidence based assessment, not a guarantee. Any method of establishing identity, including a human being looking at a face, can be mistaken in either direction. That is why each result is returned with the reasons behind it and why the outcome can be set to pause for a second check rather than to refuse outright, so a person decides the difficult cases rather than being told the answer. content.text: DPDP Consent Framework Opens New Era of Digital Trust | FaceOff Technologies | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Newsroom / Dpdp Consent Framework Opens New Era Of Digital Trust Newsroom Nov 15, 2026 DPDP Consent Framework Opens New Era of Digital Trust Share: f 𝕏 in India has reached another important milestone in its digital privacy journey with the Consent Manager registration framework under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, becoming effective on November 13, 2026. MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan inaugurated the online registration portal, dpbi.gov.in, allowing eligible Indian companies to apply for registration as Consent Managers with the Data Protection Board of India. The initiative represents a significant shift toward empowering individuals, known as Data Principals, to exercise greater control over how their personal information is collected, processed, and shared. Registered Consent Managers will serve as trusted intermediaries, enabling individuals to grant, review, manage, and withdraw consent through accessible, transparent, and interoperable digital platforms. Unlike conventional consent mechanisms, this framework emphasizes accountability to individuals rather than businesses, strengthening transparency and user-centric privacy governance across India's expanding digital ecosystem. To qualify, applicants must be incorporated in India, demonstrate adequate technical and operational capabilities, and maintain a minimum net worth of ₹2 crore, ensuring financial stability and institutional credibility. The Data Protection Board will assess applications against regulatory requirements before granting registration. Details of approved Consent Managers will be publicly available, promoting transparency and regulatory accountability. For India's technology industry, the development creates opportunities for privacy-tech companies, cybersecurity providers, system integrators, and managed service providers to develop scalable consent management and compliance solutions. However, implementation challenges remain. Enterprises must ensure secure consent records, seamless interoperability, effective withdrawal mechanisms, and integration with existing IT infrastructure while preventing misuse of personal information. The bigger picture is the emergence of privacy as a competitive differentiator. With major DPDP compliance obligations scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027, organizations must move beyond regulatory checklists toward privacy-by-design architectures. The Consent Manager framework could become a critical foundation for strengthening consumer confidence, responsible data governance, and sustainable growth in India's digital economy. content.text: FaceOff Technologies: Building Cognitive Defence Shield Against | FaceOff Technologies | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Newsroom / Faceoff Technologies Building Cognitive Defence Shield Against Ai Warfare Newsroom Nov 10, 2026 FaceOff Technologies: Building Cognitive Defence Shield Against AI Warfare Share: f 𝕏 in As cyber warfare evolves from attacking networks to manipulating human minds, FaceOff Technologies is developing a sovereign AI-powered defence ecosystem to counter cyber-enabled cognitive warfare, synthetic deception and digital manipulation. Cyber-enabled cognitive warfare represents a dangerous convergence of artificial intelligence, psychological manipulation, misinformation and cyberattacks. Unlike conventional threats targeting infrastructure, these operations attempt to influence perception, undermine institutional credibility and manipulate critical decisions through deepfakes, cloned voices, synthetic identities and coordinated disinformation. India's indigenous deep-tech company, FaceOff Technologies , is addressing this emerging challenge through its proprietary Adaptive Cognito Engine (ACE®) , combining multimodal intelligence, behavioural biometrics, facial analysis, voice authentication and contextual risk assessment to strengthen digital trust. Beyond its existing deepfake detection and identity verification capabilities, FaceOff is advancing three additional readiness areas to strengthen cognitive defence. 1. Cognitive Threat Intelligence and OSINT Readiness Through TrustShield OSINT and identity intelligence, FaceOff is developing capabilities to investigate suspicious digital identities, impersonation networks, fabricated personas and potentially coordinated influence campaigns. Cross-platform correlation and contextual analysis can help investigators identify deceptive activity while preserving human oversight. 2. Autonomous AI Agent and Behavioural Defence FaceOff's behavioural intelligence and continuous authentication capabilities can support the detection of suspicious interactions, identity misuse and abnormal activity. Its evolving AI governance approach aims to strengthen oversight of autonomous agents through risk monitoring, policy enforcement and explainable decisions. 3. Sovereign Cognitive Security and Forensic Readiness FaceOff's on-premises, edge and isolated deployment architecture enables sensitive institutions to retain control over their information. Multimodal forensic analysis, evidence preservation and post-quantum security capabilities strengthen readiness for investigations involving manipulated communications and synthetic media. Together, these capabilities could support defence establishments, law enforcement agencies, financial institutions, critical infrastructure operators and government organisations confronting AI-enabled deception. However, effective cognitive warfare defence requires more than technological detection. It demands coordinated intelligence, validated forensic evidence, privacy safeguards, institutional preparedness and responsible human decision-making. FaceOff's vision is to move cybersecurity beyond protecting systems towards protecting identity, information integrity and human judgement. The next battlefield is cognitive. The next defence frontier is digital trust. FaceOff Technologies — Verify Before You Trust. content.text: Nvidia CEO Exit Shakes AI Industry | FaceOff Technologies | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Newsroom / Nvidia Ceo Exit Shakes Ai Industry Newsroom Nov 15, 2026 Nvidia CEO Exit Shakes AI Industry Share: f 𝕏 in Nvidia faces an unprecedented leadership crisis following reports that co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and board member on November 12, 2026, ending his 33-year tenure. The reported departure followed an independent board investigation into Huang's admitted extramarital affair and allegations involving a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence. According to the reports, Nvidia's board convened Wednesday evening before announcing Huang's resignation Thursday morning, ahead of Wall Street's opening bell. The controversy intensified after The New York Times reportedly disclosed another relationship involving Huang and a senior Nvidia executive, raising additional corporate governance concerns. Separately, questions emerged regarding Alice Huang's reported association with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company examined over China's access to advanced Nvidia processors. However, allegations of espionage or improper technology transfers involving Huang remain unproven. The distinction between personal misconduct allegations and national security violations is critically important. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, transforming graphics processing technology originally designed for gaming into the foundation of today's artificial intelligence revolution. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a dominant supplier of AI accelerators, powering hyperscale data centers, generative AI platforms, and advanced computing infrastructure worldwide. The company's financial expansion has been extraordinary, with reported annual revenue rising from $27 billion in fiscal 2023 to $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026. Its data center division reportedly generated $89 billion during the second quarter of fiscal 2027, highlighting Nvidia's growing dependence on AI infrastructure spending. Nevertheless, investor confidence has weakened amid concerns that massive investments in GPUs, data centers, and AI platforms may not deliver sustainable returns. Nvidia's market valuation reportedly retreated from approximately $5.8 trillion as technology stocks faced selling pressure and investors reassessed AI-related capital expenditure. Political uncertainty surrounding semiconductor export controls, data center regulations, and US-China technology competition has further complicated the company's outlook. Meanwhile, competitors AMD, Broadcom, and Qualcomm reportedly gained during early trading, suggesting investors were reassessing competitive opportunities within the semiconductor industry. The larger question is whether Nvidia can sustain its technological dominance amid leadership uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and AI investment concerns. Its future will depend on governance, innovation, supply-chain resilience, and measurable returns from the global AI boom. content.text: UK Regulator Bets on Quantum to Fight Fraud | FaceOff Technologies | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Newsroom / Uk Regulator Bets On Quantum To Fight Fraud Newsroom Nov 10, 2026 UK Regulator Bets on Quantum to Fight Fraud Share: f 𝕏 in The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is exploring quantum computing as a potential weapon against financial crime, signalling a new direction in combating money laundering, banking fraud, and increasingly sophisticated financial threats. The regulator has announced the Quantum Experimentation Group (QEG) , a pioneering initiative bringing together financial institutions, quantum technology providers, and national research laboratories. Scheduled to launch in the first quarter of 2027, it aims to investigate practical quantum applications. The initiative will initially focus on quantum machine learning (QML) to identify suspicious financial transactions, detect hidden fraud patterns, and potentially improve anti-money laundering systems. Unlike conventional approaches, quantum techniques could eventually help analyse complex relationships across large transaction networks. To overcome data-access challenges, the FCA will provide participants with synthetic datasets, enabling controlled experimentation without exposing actual customer information. Researchers will compare quantum approaches with conventional computing techniques to assess their effectiveness. Jessica Rusu, FCA's Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer, emphasised the importance of early experimentation to identify where quantum technologies could deliver meaningful improvements. The initiative will also help regulators understand technical limitations, operational challenges, and future regulatory implications. British banks are already exploring similar opportunities. NatWest has joined quantum innovation research focused on financial crime , while Lloyds Banking Group collaborated with IBM to investigate quantum-powered detection of money mule accounts, a growing concern across international banking networks. However, quantum computing remains an emerging technology, with practical limitations involving hardware reliability, scalability, and processing costs. Its superiority over established fraud detection systems has not yet been demonstrated broadly. Financial institutions must therefore balance experimentation with cybersecurity resilience and preparations for post-quantum cryptography. For India, the initiative offers an important lesson. As digital payments, UPI transactions, synthetic identity fraud, and money mule networks expand, quantum-assisted analytics could eventually complement AI-powered fraud detection. The real opportunity lies in combining advanced computing, behavioural intelligence, secure digital identities, and regulatory collaboration to build a more resilient financial ecosystem. content.text: Eye Tracking Analysis | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Platform / Eye Tracking Emotion Detection capability Eye Tracking Analysis Gaze behaviour, fixation, and pupil response are analysed as visible signals of emotional state, with changes in eye movement and gaze patterns considered over time. Run a free analysis See all eight capabilities Eye Tracking Emotion Analysis analyses gaze behaviour, fixation, and pupil response to identify visible cues associated with emotional states. The capability considers changes in how a person looks, focuses, and moves their eyes rather than relying only on a single still frame. Different emotional states can be reflected through different gaze and pupil patterns. Happiness can appear through steady focus and dilated pupils. Anger can be associated with piercing stares and fewer blinks, while sadness can appear through a downward gaze and slower blinking. Surprise can be reflected through rapid pupil shifts. Fear can appear through erratic gaze patterns and quick, frequent blinks. By considering these visible eye and gaze patterns, Eye Tracking Analysis provides an additional signal for understanding emotional state within the wider multimodal platform. Eye Tracking Analysis is one of eight signals used by the Trust Factor Engine. It is considered alongside the other seven rather than being treated as the only basis for the overall result. A single signal does not independently determine the final verdict. content.text: Facial Emotion Recognition | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Platform / Facial Emotion Recognition Detection capability Facial Emotion Recognition Facial muscle movement and visible expression patterns are tracked over time to identify emotional cues that may not be clear from a single still frame. Run a free analysis See all eight capabilities Facial Emotion Recognition analyses visible facial expressions and the muscle patterns associated with them over time. Instead of relying on a single still image, it considers how facial features move and change while an expression is being made. Different emotions can be reflected through different visible facial cues. Happiness can appear through smiling and raised cheeks. Anger can be associated with tense brows and lips, while sadness can appear through drooping facial features and fewer blinks. Surprise can involve widened eyes and a dropped jaw. Fear can appear through a stretched mouth and darting eyes, while disgust can be reflected through a wrinkled nose and raised lips.By examining these visible expression patterns over time, the capability provides a way to interpret facial emotional cues that may be missed when only a single frame is considered. Facial Emotion Recognition is one of eight signals used by the Trust Factor Engine. It is considered alongside the other seven rather than being treated as the only basis for the overall result. A single signal does not independently determine the final verdict. content.text: Posture & Behaviour | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Platform / Posture Behavioral Detection capability Posture & Behaviour Posture and Behaviour analysis reads how a person holds and moves their body across a video, turning visible physical cues into one of the eight signals behind a FaceOff trust result. Run a free analysis See all eight capabilities What it is The body says something the face alone does not Posture and Behaviour is one of the eight detection capabilities that make up the FaceOff platform. It looks at visible body position and movement in a video and identifies the physical cues people commonly associate with different emotional states. The important word is visible. Nothing is inferred from anything a viewer could not also see on screen. It also watches how a position changes rather than judging a single moment. A person can look tense in one frame and relaxed a second later, so a still image is a weak place to draw a conclusion. Happiness may show as relaxed shoulders and an upright stance. Anger may show as clenched fists and a forward lean. Sadness may show as slouching and a lowered head, surprise as lifted shoulders, fear as freezing or leaning back, and disgust as twisting away or physically withdrawing. Read across a whole clip, those changes become a signal that supports the wider result. One of eight signals in the Trust Factor Engine. It contributes to a result and never decides one on its own. How the weighting works Worth knowing Body language is evidence, not a verdict. What this capability produces is an observation the platform weighs alongside seven others. Happiness Anger Sadness Surprise Fear Disgust The six states with physical cues the body tends to show. How it works From a video to an observation you can act on 01 Submit Send a video the way that suits you: upload a file, connect a live feed, or pass it in from a system your team already uses. 02 Observe The person's body position and movement are followed across the whole clip rather than sampled from one frame. 03 Interpret Changes in stance and movement are matched to the physical cues commonly associated with each emotional state. 04 Combine The observation joins the seven other signals in the Trust Factor Engine, which weighs them together rather than in isolation. 05 Explain You receive a result in everyday language, with the moments in the video that shaped it, so a reviewer can check the reasoning. What it gives you Ordered by what changes a review first Movement read across time A stance is judged by how it changes through the clip, not by how it looked in the frame someone happened to pause on. Whole clip, not one frame Six emotional states from the body Happiness, anger, sadness, surprise, fear and disgust each have physical cues the capability is built to recognise. Recognised from posture alone Works with the video you already have Recorded files, live feeds and video arriving from your existing systems are all handled the same way. No special camera and no studio. No new hardware needed Always part of a wider picture The finding is presented as one signal among eight, so nobody is asked to act on body language on its own. One of eight signals Explained in everyday language Results are written for the person reviewing the case rather than for a specialist, and they point at what was seen and when. Readable by any reviewer Explore the eight signals See where posture sits among the other seven Select any signal to see what it looks at and what it adds. The Trust Factor Engine adjusts how much weight each one carries depending on what a particular video can support, so the mix is never fixed and no single signal is ever the whole answer. Deepfake Detection Whether the face and the footage show signs of being made or altered Facial Emotion Recognition Expression as it moves and settles, rather than a single look Eye Tracking Analysis Where the gaze goes, how it rests and how it shifts Posture & Behaviour This page Body position and movement, read across the whole clip Heart Rate from Video Pulse estimated from the face, showing what an expression can hide Speech Sentiment Rhythm and delivery of speech, separate from the words themselves Audio Tone Sentiment The emotional colour underneath the voice Oxygen Saturation A further physical reading taken from the same footage You are here Posture & Behaviour Body position and movement, read across the whole clip . A clear result comes from several signals agreeing. Where they disagree, the engine says so rather than picking a side quietly. Where it is used Anywhere a recorded person has to be understood, not just identified Banking and insurance Recorded claim statements and video calls carry more than words. Body language gives reviewers another reason to look closer at a claim, or to move it along with confidence. Law enforcement Interview and body worn footage can be reviewed for behavioural cues that help investigators decide which recordings deserve a second look. Courts and legal Video evidence arrives with an explanation of what was observed and when, which supports a reviewer preparing or examining a case. Healthcare In remote consultations, visible signs of distress or discomfort can be surfaced to a clinician who is watching a screen rather than a room. Education Remote assessment and supervision benefit from an extra, visible signal about how a candidate is behaving throughout a session. Customer intelligence Recorded conversations and video feedback can be understood in terms of how people reacted, not only what they said. Why FaceOff Eight signals, one result, and the reasoning left visible No single signal decides anything Eight capabilities are considered together, with the weight adjusted to what the footage can support. A result has to convince more than one of them. A score with room in it The Trust Factor Engine returns a graded trust level rather than a flat yes or no, so borderline cases look borderline instead of being forced into a box. You can see why Every result comes with the observations behind it in ordinary language, so your team reviews findings rather than trusting a number. It fits how you already work The same capability serves an uploaded file, a live feed or a system you already run, so checks happen inside normal work. Common questions Frequently asked questions What is posture and behaviour analysis? − Posture and behaviour analysis is a way of reading visible body position and movement in a video to identify the physical cues people associate with different emotional states. In FaceOff it is one of eight detection capabilities, and it studies how a stance changes through a clip rather than judging a single frame. Can body language tell you if someone is lying? + No, and FaceOff does not claim it can. This capability reports what is visible in the way a person holds and moves their body. It is one input among eight, and it is designed to help a human reviewer decide where to look, not to reach a conclusion about honesty on anybody's behalf. Which emotions can be recognised from posture? + Six: happiness, anger, sadness, surprise, fear and disgust. Each has physical cues that tend to appear in the body, such as an upright and relaxed stance, a forward lean, a lowered head, lifted shoulders, leaning back, or turning away. Does it work on video we already have? + Yes. Recorded files, live feeds and video passed in from systems your teams already use are all supported. No special camera, sensor or recording setup is required. How does this fit with the other seven capabilities? + It contributes one signal to the Trust Factor Engine, which weighs all eight together. The engine adjusts how much each signal counts based on what a given video can support, so a result reflects several capabilities agreeing rather than one speaking alone. Do we have to be technical to read the results? + No. Findings are written in everyday language and point at the moments in the video that shaped them, so the person handling the case can review the reasoning without specialist training. content.text: Privacy By Design | FaceOff Technologies | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu LEGAL Privacy By Design Privacy Preservation and Secure API Model in Faceoff Faceoff is designed to preserve data privacy and confidentiality by offering companies only an API for video analysis, without offering any cloud storage or video handling infrastructure. This design ensures that customer videos never leave their own secure environments. Faceoff does not store, view, or access any video data. Instead, Faceoff only monitors API usage metrics (number of videos processed) without seeing or saving the content. Zero Video Storage Local VPC Inference Stateless Execution CUSTOMER ENVIRONMENT Private VPC / Sovereign Infrastructure AIR-GAPPED ▶ Customer Video Feed Upload & Process Entirely Within Your Cloud LOCAL INGEST Faceoff API / SDK REST API / Container Analyzing Locally IN-MEMORY ✓ Trust Score & Model Outputs Returned Internally & Discarded in Memory LOCAL VERDICT VIDEO NEVER LEAVES CUSTOMER ENVIRONMENT Outbound Telemetry (Usage Logs Only) Zero Video Content Endpoint API Usage → Epoch Timestamp → State Status → Counter Video Count SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE & WORKFLOW Privacy by Architecture Dual-enclave topology separating in-perimeter video computation from remote metadata licensing. CUSTOMER INFRASTRUCTURE AWS / Azure / GCP / Private Cloud / On-Premise AWS Azure GCP Private Cloud Executed Inside Your Environment: Video Uploaded & stored locally only Customer Cloud Processing On-the-fly ephemeral execution Volatile RAM Frames Zero frame extraction to outside Internal Buffer Audio Voice biometric consistency checks Zero Egress Trust Score Returned directly to your app Local Verdict Data Sovereignty: 100% Zero Cloud Interaction Beyond Count AIR-GAP BOUNDARY NO VIDEO NO FRAMES NO BIOMETRIC DATA Usage Metrics Only FACEOFF Central Server & Usage Telemetry Stored Media Content: 0 Bytes AUTHENTICATED Monitored Telemetry Only: API Usage Metrics Number of videos processed count API Count API Key Binds usage to company ID Authentication Timestamp API endpoint hit epoch time UTC Sync Request Status Success / Failure / Error log HTTP Status Statistical Records Only Never User Content Architecture and Workflow Sequence: 1. Deploy In Customer Cloud Faceoff provides a lightweight, secure REST API / SDK that companies deploy inside AWS, Azure, GCP, or private cloud. 2. Local Upload & Processing Companies upload and process video streams entirely within their own infrastructure perimeter. 3. Internal Trust Scoring The API endpoint internally analyzes video, generating trust scores and model outputs locally. 4. Minimal Metadata Notify Faceoff central server is only notified of API call metadata. No video, frames, or biometric features are ever transmitted. TECHNICAL MECHANISMS ENSURING PRIVACY Five Privacy Principles Architectural guarantees enforced across every SDK, API container, and enterprise deployment. 01 01 — Data Localization Video remains inside the customer's environment. The video remains inside the company's environment. The Faceoff API container/module executes locally with zero upload of video to external servers and no external cloud interaction beyond API usage count. 02 02 — Minimal API Communication Only essential usage metadata is communicated. Faceoff API only sends usage logs: Timestamp, API endpoint hit, Status (Success/Failure/Error), and Metadata (Company ID, number of videos processed). No video payload or video metadata (filename, user data, camera info) are sent outside. 03 03 — Stateless Processing Video is processed on-the-fly and discarded after processing. Each video input is processed on-the-fly in volatile RAM. After processing, the video content is immediately discarded in memory with zero persistent storage. 04 04 — Secure Authentication Unique API keys identify and authenticate companies. Companies are issued unique API keys for authentication. The API key helps bind usage tracking to a specific company without needing to access the actual data. 05 05 — Auditability Organizations can inspect and audit their local deployment. Companies can audit Faceoff's deployment locally. Faceoff publishes a transparent technical whitepaper describing exactly what data is (and is not) transmitted or saved. Usage Metering Mechanism Tracking Video Count Without Accessing Data Every API call is counted via an internal trigger whenever a video is processed. Faceoff maintains only statistical records of usage, never user content. What Faceoff Counts: • Number of API requests (videos analyzed) • Associated company API key • Exact timestamp of request • Internal execution status code What Faceoff Never Receives: • No video frames or raw video payload • No audio streams or transcripts • No biometric embeddings or face vectors • No metadata (filenames, camera info, user IDs) DETAILED ARCHITECTURAL MATRIX Why This Approach Is Highly Privacy-Preserving 10 Technical Dimensions Aspect Traditional Cloud-Based Systems Faceoff API-Based Private Deployment Data Residency Videos are transmitted to and stored on third-party cloud infrastructure, often outside organizational control. Videos remain within the organization's secure environment; no external transmission or storage. Privacy Risk High risk due to centralized storage and third-party access, increasing vulnerability to breaches and misuse. Ultra-low risk: Faceoff does not receive or access video data; full control remains with the data owner. Compliance Complexity Data movement across jurisdictions can raise compliance challenges (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA). Simplified compliance as data never leaves the organization's infrastructure or regional boundaries. Trust Model Requires trust in third-party cloud provider's security, policies, and access controls. Trustless by design: Faceoff operates entirely within the client's infrastructure; zero data visibility. Data Ownership Cloud providers may store and potentially access user data, raising concerns around ownership and consent. Complete data ownership and custody retained by the client organization at all times. Latency and Performance Dependent on internet speed and remote processing; may experience network bottlenecks. Local processing ensures faster response times, reduced latency, and high availability. Deployment Flexibility Tied to provider's infrastructure and policies; limited customizability. Highly modular: deployable on any cloud, hybrid, or on-premise setup under full client control. System Auditing Limited transparency into backend operations; difficult to fully audit data flow. Full auditability: organizations can inspect and validate API behavior locally. Scalability Scales with provider cost; often incurs increasing fees with usage. Scales with organization's own infrastructure; predictable cost and usage metrics. Usage Tracking Full visibility by provider, including data content, user behavior, and volume. Only aggregate usage statistics (e.g., number of API calls) are shared with Faceoff. No data content is tracked. Complete architectural independence with zero media egress. Client retains 100% data custody at all times. REGULATORY ALIGNMENT Compliance Readiness Because Faceoff never accesses user data, it naturally aligns with global regulatory standards. Companies using Faceoff can certify privacy compliance easily. GDPR Art. 25 & 32 Ready General Data Protection Regulation Because video is processed locally, zero cross-border data transfer occurs. Full compliance with data minimization & storage limitation mandates. HIPAA PHI Shielded Health Insurance Portability & Accountability Telemedicine and patient biometric streams never leave covered entity infrastructure, eliminating external BAA exposure risks. ISO/IEC 27001 Controls Aligned Information Security Management Strictly aligns with standard-defined access control, local perimeter security, and air-gapped isolation controls. CCPA / CPRA Zero Retention California Consumer Privacy Act Zero retention, profiling, or secondary sale of consumer biometric identifiers or personal video records. DATA SOVEREIGNTY GUARANTEE Your Data Stays Yours. Faceoff is designed to analyze video without taking ownership or custody of the video itself. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 8(6) In the event of a personal data breach, intimate the Data Protection Board and each affected Data Principal in the form and manner prescribed. Incident scope resolves through the catalogue into the exact list of affected Principals, and intimations to both the Board and each Principal are generated, tracked and evidenced from that list. Sec. 8(5) Take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach. Safeguards are evidenced continuously before an incident rather than reconstructed after one — which is what makes the defence available when the Board asks. Sec. 2(u) A personal data breach includes unauthorised processing, accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access. The definition is broader than exfiltration, so detection covers unauthorised internal processing and loss of access, not only external attack. Sec. 28 The Board may inquire into a breach and determine whether penalty is warranted, taking account of mitigating action taken promptly. The full incident trail — detection, containment, remediation and intimation, each timestamped — is the record the Board weighs when assessing mitigation. Sec. 33 Penalty is determined by the nature, gravity and duration of the breach, the type of data affected, repetition, and mitigating action. Every factor the Board weighs is a field in the incident record, so the mitigation argument is evidenced rather than narrated after the fact. Exposure avoided Up to ₹250 Cr for failing to prevent a breach and a further ₹200 Cr for failing to intimate it — the two largest items in the Schedule, and they can attach to the same incident. content.text: Consent Management — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Obtain, record and enforce explicit consent before you process personal data Consent Management · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 5, 6, 9 Book a DPDP walkthrough Obtain, record and manage explicit permission for every processing purpose — across every channel, in every jurisdiction, from a single record of truth. Platform capabilities Purpose-level consent ledger Multi-language notice engine Real-time enforcement API Notice languages served 23 Notice languages served Consent check at query time < 1s Consent check at query time Purposes with a receipt 100% Purposes with a receipt Blanket consents possible 0 Blanket consents possible Figures illustrative. How consent moves One consent signal, every channel, every system that processes Consent is collected wherever your customers already are, normalised into a single purpose-scoped record, and pushed to the systems that touch personal data — each of which acknowledges it before it processes. Capture channels Web & cookie banner Captured at first touch Mobile app SDK In-app preference centre API & server System-to-system capture Agent, IVR & branch Assisted and voice journeys Paper & thumb impression Digitised at ingestion Consent engine 01 Gateway One entry point for every channel 02 Normalise Channel formats to one consent object 03 Policy & purpose Scoped to a purpose and a notice version 04 Consent ledger Append-only, timestamped, replayable 05 Event publisher Change fans out in real time Downstream systems CRM & MDM Checks before it contacts ack Analytics & BI Checks before it models ack Processors & vendors Inherits and confirms ack Data warehouse Checks before it joins ack Ad & martech Checks before it targets ack Withdrawal runs the same path in reverse. Every hop — the notice served, the choice made, the policy version applied and each downstream acknowledgement — lands in an append-only trail you can replay. Capability What Consent Management does Transparency & communication Plain-language notice at the point of collection, plus a self-service centre where an individual can see and change every consent given. Notice templates versioned per purpose 22 Eighth Schedule languages plus English Every notice served is replayable Preference centre in any channel Granular consent & control Purpose-level opt-in rather than a single blanket toggle — and withdrawal made exactly as easy as the original consent. Consent object scoped to one purpose Affirmative capture with timestamp Consent bound to the notice version shown One-click withdrawal, parity enforced Automated & centralised management One consent store, updated in real time, that every downstream system must query before it processes. Real-time consent API at query time Event fan-out to processors on change Consent Manager-ready interoperability Age-band gating and guardian flows Outcome Consent that is not merely recorded but enforced — every downstream system checks before it processes, and withdrawal actually stops the processing. DPDP alignment Consent Management — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 5 Itemised notice describing the personal data, the purpose, how to exercise rights and how to complain to the Board — in English or any Eighth Schedule language. A templated notice engine renders per purpose, versioned and localised into all 22 scheduled languages. Every notice served is stored and replayable against the Principal who saw it. Sec. 6(1) Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, by clear affirmative action, limited to data necessary for the specified purpose. Consent is captured as a purpose-scoped object with an affirmative-action event, an immutable timestamp and a binding to the exact notice version displayed. Blanket consent is structurally impossible. Sec. 6(4)–(6) Withdrawal must be as easy as giving. Processing must cease within a reasonable time, and processors must be made to cease too. One-click withdrawal with click-parity enforced against the give-flow. Revocation fans out to every processor that inherited the consent; cessation is tracked to an SLA and evidenced. Sec. 6(7)–(9) A Consent Manager registered with the Board must give the Principal an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform to manage consent. Consent artefacts are emitted in an interoperable format with Consent Manager-ready APIs, so registration and integration are configuration rather than a rebuild. Sec. 9 Verifiable parental consent for children and persons with a guardian; no tracking or behavioural advertising directed at children. Age-band assurance gates the flow into a guardian consent path, and a child flag suppresses tracking and behavioural advertising downstream automatically. Exposure avoided Sec. 9 failures carry up to ₹200 Cr under the Schedule. Consent defects also invalidate the lawful basis for every downstream processing activity — one control gap becomes estate-wide exposure. content.text: Cookie Management — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Discover, classify and gate cookies before they track your visitors Cookie Management · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 6(1) Book a DPDP walkthrough A continuous governance loop that finds cookies, classifies them, gates them behind consent and watches for drift. Shipped as part of Consent Management. Platform capabilities Scheduled estate-wide scanning AI + rules classification Prior-blocking script Known cookies catalogued 98.7% Known cookies catalogued Scan-to-policy refresh < 24h Scan-to-policy refresh Tags gated pre-consent 100% Tags gated pre-consent Categories auto-mapped 4 Categories auto-mapped Figures illustrative. How it works Cookie Management, end to end Five repeatable stages turn raw discovery into a live, geo-aware banner that blocks before it asks, then keep watching for drift 01 Scan Crawl pages, SPAs, subdomains and authenticated journeys 02 Classify Map each cookie to category, vendor, purpose and duration 03 Generate Build the banner UI and the auto-block script 04 Deploy One snippet, or through your tag manager 05 Monitor Re-scan, detect drift, refresh the policy Non-essential tags stay dormant until the visitor opts in, the default-deny behaviour Sec. 6(1) requires. Capability What Cookie Management does Deep scanning Scheduled crawls across pages, SPAs, subdomains and authenticated journeys find every cookie, pixel, tag and storage entry. Single-page apps and authenticated journeys Subdomain and multi-property coverage Pixels, tags and local storage, not just cookies Scheduled rescans rather than a one-off audit Auto-classification & prior blocking AI and rules map each cookie to Necessary, Functional, Analytics or Marketing — and non-essential tags stay dormant until the visitor opts in. Vendor, purpose and duration resolved per cookie Default-deny behaviour regulators expect Equal Accept and Reject prominence No pre-ticked boxes, granular per-category toggles Drift monitoring New or rogue cookies trigger DPO alerts and auto-refresh the cookie policy and banner declarations. Alerts on cookies no scan previously saw Policy and declarations refreshed automatically Geo-targeted banners for DPDP, GDPR and CCPA Withdrawal as easy as the original consent Outcome The banner stops being a decorative overlay and becomes an enforcement point — nothing non-essential fires before the affirmative action. DPDP alignment Cookie Management — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 6(1) Consent must be by clear affirmative action, and processing may not begin before it is given. Prior blocking is the control that makes this real: a tag firing before the affirmative action means processing began without consent, and no receipt can retrofit it. Sec. 6(4) Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. The banner exposes a persistent re-open control with equal Accept and Reject prominence, so withdrawal is the same number of clicks as the original grant. Sec. 5 Notice must itemise what is collected and for what purpose. Cookie declarations are generated from the live scan, so the published policy matches what the site actually sets rather than what it set at launch. Exposure avoided A tag that fires pre-consent is unlawful processing from the first pageview, and it is the single easiest defect for a regulator or a journalist to verify from outside your perimeter. content.text: Intelligent Data Mapper — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Discover, classify and map personal data across your entire enterprise estate Intelligent Data Mapper · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 8(3), 8(7) Book a DPDP walkthrough You cannot protect, redact, erase or report on what you have not found. Discovery locates and classifies personal and sensitive data across the entire estate. Platform capabilities Continuous estate-wide scanning AI classification models Identity-resolved catalogue Documents scanned in a single run 1,148 Documents scanned in a single run Actionable findings, not raw inventory 546 Actionable findings, not raw inventory Frameworks scored in parallel 6 Frameworks scored in parallel Figures illustrative. How it works Intelligent Data Mapper, end to end A continuous pipeline replaces the stale inventory: find, parse, classify and reason over every document in the estate, on a schedule rather than on a project plan 01 Task router Scheduled and event-triggered scans across connected sources 02 Ingestion Structured, semi-structured and unstructured stores 03 Parsing & OCR Documents, images and free text made readable 04 Detection Heuristic, neural and consensus layers score each candidate 05 Deep intelligence Context-aware reasoning with provenance retained 06 Reporting Actionable findings and per-framework posture Output is what needs action, not an inventory nobody reads, and every finding carries the chain that produced it. Capability What Intelligent Data Mapper does Systematic detection & management Continuous scanning of structured and unstructured sources, with automated classification and ongoing monitoring rather than a one-off inventory. Structured, unstructured and semi-structured Scheduled and event-triggered rescans Drift detection as new stores appear Identity resolution across systems AI-powered accuracy Models that confirm sensitive data with high precision and adapt as new data patterns and regulatory definitions emerge. Context-aware classification, not regex Confidence scoring with human review Retraining as new patterns emerge Extensible to new data categories Data integrity & compliance Invalid and stale elements are flagged and corrected, and every scan leaves a detailed audit trail. Accuracy and staleness flagging Lineage from source to consumer Detailed audit trail per scan Feeds DSAR, redaction and erasure Outcome A live catalogue that answers "where is this person's data?" as a query — which is what makes every rights, erasure and breach obligation achievable inside its clock. DPDP alignment Intelligent Data Mapper — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 8(3) Ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency of personal data where it is used to make a decision affecting the Principal or is disclosed to another Data Fiduciary. Discovery maps every copy of an attribute across the estate and flags divergence between them, so accuracy is measured against all copies rather than the system of record alone. Sec. 8(7) Erase personal data on withdrawal of consent or when the purpose is no longer being served, unless retention is legally required. The catalogue returns every store holding a given Principal's data, so erasure runs against a complete list — and the completeness itself is evidenced rather than assumed. Sec. 5 Notice must itemise the personal data being collected — which requires knowing what is actually collected. Discovery reconciles the data declared in notice against the data actually present, surfacing collection that no notice covers. Sec. 11–12 The Principal may obtain a summary of personal data held and processing activities, and may request correction, completion, updating and erasure. Access and correction resolve against a live, identity-resolved catalogue instead of a manual hunt across systems and owners. Sec. 8(6) Breach intimation must reach every affected Data Principal. When an incident is scoped to systems, the catalogue converts that into the exact list of affected Principals — turning notification from an investigation into a query. Exposure avoided Erasure and accuracy failures sit in the ₹50 Cr residual band, but the greater exposure is derivative: without discovery, Sec. 8(6), 11 and 12 all become undeliverable inside their statutory windows.
