content.text: Data Anonymization & Masking — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Mask and redact sensitive data so it stays usable without exposing the individual Data Anonymization & Masking · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 8(4), 8(5) Book a DPDP walkthrough Obscure sensitive information inside live data sets so the data stays usable — for analytics, testing, support and disclosure — without exposing the individual. Platform capabilities Static & dynamic masking AI detection in free text Role and purpose-aware rules How it works Data Anonymization & Masking, end to end One governed source, many masked derivatives. The estates most likely to be breached stop holding raw personal data at all Source of truth Production data Rules applied by role, purpose and context: format-preserving where analytics need it, consistent tokens where joins do. What downstream actually receives Non-production Test and staging hold no raw personal data Analytics Joinable, but no longer identifying Vendor extracts Processor exposure bounded by design DSAR responses Third-party data redacted automatically Sec. 8(5): reasonable security safeguards. Masking reduces the population at risk instead of only defending it. Capability What Data Anonymization & Masking does Comprehensive enterprise solution Handles large volumes, adapts to new categories of personal data, and integrates with existing storage and processing infrastructure. Scales to enterprise data volumes Adapts to new personal data categories Integrates with existing pipelines Static masking and dynamic redaction AI-powered redaction Detects, identifies and redacts against defined criteria with far greater precision and speed than rule-only approaches. Context-aware detection in free text Documents, images and logs covered Precision tuned per data category Consistent tokens preserve joinability Custom redaction mechanisms Protocols tuned to the nature and context of the data, automated by rule, with rules that are easy to update as policy changes. Rules by role, purpose and context Format-preserving where analytics need it Policy changes without a code release Every redaction decision logged Outcome A smaller blast radius before anything goes wrong — non-production, analytics and vendor estates stop holding raw personal data at all. DPDP alignment Data Anonymization & Masking — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 8(4) Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure effective observance of the Act. Masking is enforced as a technical control at the data layer rather than a policy instruction to teams, so observance does not depend on individual discipline. Sec. 8(5) Take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach. Data masked in non-production, analytics and vendor estates cannot be breached in those estates — the safeguard reduces the population at risk instead of only defending it. Sec. 8(1)–(2) The Fiduciary remains responsible for processing carried out by a processor engaged under contract. Masked extracts are what leaves for vendors and test environments, so processor exposure is bounded by design rather than by contract language alone. Sec. 11 The access summary must be delivered to the requesting Principal — and only to them. Third-party personal data appearing in a DSAR response is redacted automatically before release, so fulfilling one right does not breach another Principal's. Sec. 6(1) Consent is limited to the personal data necessary for the specified purpose. Masking enforces minimisation in practice: downstream consumers receive only the fields their purpose actually requires. Exposure avoided Failure to take reasonable security safeguards under Sec. 8(5) is the single largest item in the Schedule at up to ₹250 Cr. Masking is the control most directly responsive to it. content.text: DSAR Management — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Fulfil every access, correction and erasure request inside the statutory clock DSAR Management · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 11–14 Book a DPDP walkthrough Individuals have a right to see, correct and erase what you hold about them. This turns that right into a workflow with a clock, an owner and an evidence trail. Platform capabilities Automated intake & routing Catalogue-driven fulfilment Clock and SLA tracking How it works DSAR Management, end to end Every request runs the same pipeline against a clock that starts on receipt, so status is a fact drawn from the catalogue rather than an email thread 01 Intake Self-service portal, email or API: all channels land in one queue 02 Verify Identity proofed before any data is disclosed 03 Discover Catalogue returns every store holding this Principal's data 04 Redact Third-party personal data removed before release 05 Fulfil Delivered in a portable format, evidenced The statutory clock runs across all five stages, with escalation before the deadline rather than after it. Capability What DSAR Management does Access to personal data The requester sees what is held and how it is processed — assembled from the catalogue rather than from an email thread. Summary assembled from the live catalogue Processing activities disclosed with it Identities of recipients where required Delivered in a portable format Compliance & process Identity verified before disclosure, response inside the statutory window, extendable only where the law allows. Identity proofing before any disclosure Clock starts on receipt and is tracked Escalation before the deadline, not after Full trail of who accessed what Enterprise scale Automated intake and fulfilment at volume, with third-party data redacted or anonymised before release. Automated intake across channels Bulk handling without linear headcount Third-party data redacted automatically Grievance and nomination handled too Outcome Rights fulfilled inside the statutory window at volume, with the identity check, the redaction and the evidence produced as a by-product of the workflow. DPDP alignment DSAR Management — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 11 The Principal may obtain a summary of personal data being processed, the processing activities, and the identities of other Fiduciaries with whom it has been shared. The summary is generated from the live catalogue and the consent ledger, including sharing lineage — so recipients are named from records rather than reconstructed from memory. Sec. 12(1) The Principal may request correction, completion and updating of their personal data. Corrections propagate to every store the catalogue identifies, and the propagation itself is evidenced, so accuracy is fixed estate-wide rather than in one system. Sec. 12(3) The Principal may request erasure, and the Fiduciary must erase unless retention is necessary for a specified purpose or legal compliance. Erasure executes against the discovered store list; legal-hold and retention exceptions are recorded with the basis relied on, so a refusal is defensible. Sec. 13 The Fiduciary must provide a readily available grievance redressal mechanism and respond within the prescribed period. Grievances are first-class tickets with their own clock, routed to the DPO, and evidenced end to end for the Board. Sec. 14 The Principal may nominate an individual to exercise their rights in the event of death or incapacity. Nomination is captured, verified and honoured as an authorised path into the same rights workflow. Exposure avoided Rights failures fall in the residual ₹50 Cr band, but they are the most visible: every missed DSAR is a Principal with a live grievance and a direct route to the Data Protection Board. content.text: PIA / DPIA Assessment — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Evaluate and price privacy risk before software reaches production PIA / DPIA Assessment · the overview film Sound on Overview Primary DPDP sections Sec. 10(2) Book a DPDP walkthrough A systematic process to evaluate and manage the privacy risk of any project, initiative or technology that processes personal data — before it reaches production. Platform capabilities Design-phase triggering Multi-regime mapping Risk register with owners Frameworks from one description 9 Frameworks from one description Activities under live assessment 18 Activities under live assessment Answers ungrounded in your evidence 0 Answers ungrounded in your evidence Figures illustrative. How it works PIA / DPIA Assessment, end to end Describe a processing activity once, then assess it under any regime. Every answer is grounded in the evidence you uploaded One description Processing activity Nature, scope, context and purpose captured once, versioned, with necessity and proportionality tested. Nine regulatory outputs DPDP Sec. 10(2)(c) GDPR Art. 35 DPIA EU AI Act Algorithmic due diligence CPPA · LGPD · Colorado Regional equivalents UK ICO · TIA · LIA Transfer and interest tests Residual risk graded and signed off by a named owner, so “appropriate measures” is demonstrable rather than declarative. Capability What PIA / DPIA Assessment does Workflow & integration Assessments triggered from the design phase and carried through the project lifecycle, rather than retrofitted at launch. Triggered from intake or CI/CD Threshold screening decides who needs one Risks tracked to closure, not to filing Reassessment on material change Legal & regulatory frameworks One assessment mapped to GDPR DPIA, DPDP and other regimes, with documentation held ready for regulatory review. One record, many regulatory outputs Mapped to GDPR Art. 35 and DPDP Sec. 10 Documentation retained for the Board Versioned decision history Assessment process Identify what needs a PIA; assess nature, scope, context and purpose; evaluate and mitigate risk to rights and freedoms. Nature, scope, context and purpose Necessity and proportionality tested Risk to rights scored and mitigated Residual risk signed off by an owner Outcome Privacy risk found and priced before it ships — and a documented assessment record ready for a Board inquiry or an independent auditor without a scramble. DPDP alignment PIA / DPIA Assessment — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 10(2)(c)(i) A Significant Data Fiduciary must undertake periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments. Assessments run on a defined schedule per processing activity, with completion, findings and residual risk tracked as a live posture rather than an annual artefact. Sec. 10(2)(c)(ii) A Significant Data Fiduciary must undertake periodic audit. Assessment findings feed the audit workflow directly, so the auditor tests against the same record the business used to make the decision. Sec. 10(2)(a) Appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India, answerable to the board or its equivalent. The DPO is a first-class role in the workflow with named approval gates, so accountability is recorded per decision rather than asserted in a policy. Sec. 10(2)(c)(iii) Undertake such other measures as prescribed, including due diligence of algorithmic software that may risk the rights of Data Principals. Algorithmic due diligence is a dedicated assessment type covering model purpose, training data provenance, bias testing and human oversight. Sec. 8(4) Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure effective observance of the Act. Every mitigation decision is recorded against the processing activity it protects, so “appropriate measures” is demonstrable rather than declarative. Exposure avoided Sec. 10 failures carry up to ₹150 Cr. SDF notification is at the Central Government's discretion by class of fiduciary — an enterprise can become subject to these duties without changing anything it does. content.text: Privacy Program Governance — Data Privacy | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Data Privacy / Privacy Governance Data Privacy · Module 08 Privacy Program Governance The control plane over the whole programme — how data is collected, stored, processed and shared, and who is accountable for each of those. Book a DPDP walkthrough All Data Privacy Platform capabilities Multi-regime control library Processor & vendor register Retention and transfer controls Primary DPDP sections Sec. 4, 7, 10, 16 How it works Privacy Program Governance, end to end Regulation is expressed as configuration over a shared control library, so the next regime is a mapping rather than another eighteen-month programme Regimes Each expressed as configuration, not as a separate build. DPDP GDPR CCPA / CPRA LGPD PIPEDA One control library A single control can satisfy many regimes; requirements map to named owners and a posture per jurisdiction. Programme records RoPA from live systems, lawful basis per activity, processor register, retention schedules and transfer controls. Shared fabric Data catalogue, identity resolution, policy engine, AI classification and the evidence trail. Sec. 8(1) is the structural trap: the Fiduciary carries the penalty for a processor's failure. The register is what quantifies it. Capability What Privacy Program Governance does Comprehensive privacy programme One view across GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, PDPA, NESA, LGPD and DPDP, so every requirement is visible and owned. RoPA maintained from live systems One control satisfies many regimes Requirements mapped to named owners Posture visible per jurisdiction Automation & efficiency Automated tooling removes manual error from complex compliance tasks and cuts programme operating cost. Lawful basis recorded per activity Vendor and processor register Retention schedules enforced, not filed Cross-border transfer controls Transparency & trust Meets rising consumer expectation of privacy and turns compliance posture into a commercial asset. DPDP alignment Privacy Program Governance — section by section What the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires, and the control that satisfies it. Section What the Act requires How the product satisfies it Sec. 4 & 7 Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose — with consent, or for one of the listed legitimate uses. Lawful basis is recorded per processing activity and re-tested when the purpose changes, so “legitimate use” is a documented determination rather than a convenient assumption. Sec. 8(1)–(2) The Data Fiduciary is responsible for processing by a processor engaged under a valid contract, including on the Principal's behalf. A processor register ties every vendor to the activities, purposes and consents they inherit, and to the contract that permits it — so liability is mapped, not discovered. Sec. 10(1) The Central Government may notify any Data Fiduciary or class as a Significant Data Fiduciary based on volume, sensitivity and risk factors. SDF obligations are tracked as a live posture that can be switched on by class, so notification is a configuration change rather than a programme. Sec. 16 Transfer of personal data outside India is permitted except to countries restricted by the Central Government by notification. Transfer controls are evaluated against the current restricted list at processing time, with the data flow map showing where each attribute physically resides. Sec. 17 Exemptions apply for certain purposes, including legal claims, State instrumentalities and research, subject to prescribed standards. Exemptions are configured as explicit, evidenced exceptions with a named basis and owner — never as an undocumented gap in enforcement. Exposure avoided Sec. 8(1) is the structural trap: the Fiduciary carries the penalty for a processor's failure. Without a processor register mapped to purposes and consents, that exposure is unquantified. It combines a guided session, liveness assessment, identity verification and synthetic media analysis. How is it different from normal face verification? + Face verification asks whether two images appear to be the same person. BehaviorBioAuth also considers whether that person is actively participating, assessing the session throughout rather than at a single moment. How does it help against replay attacks? + The guided interactions can vary between sessions and the responses are assessed as the session runs, which makes pre-recorded or replayed attempts far harder while keeping the journey simple for genuine users. Can it detect deepfakes? + It can include synthetic media analysis that looks for indicators of AI-generated or manipulated content. The result is an additional signal for your fraud team; human review and policy still apply to higher-risk cases. Sensitive data is protected with enterprise-grade encryption, secure storage and controlled access, and your own retention and audit policies apply. Does it replace human fraud investigators? + No. It automates verification and highlights sessions needing attention. Most platforms grade the words alone. A confident delivery that will not hold eye contact surfaces as the contradiction it is. Flagship capability · three readings, one result 02 Single-pass decisioning Conventional AI interviewers take three or four sequential steps per turn, and the candidate waits out the silence. Evaluation, psychometric analysis and the next conversational move are merged into one pass, so the interviewer answers without leaving a gap for the candidate to fill. One pass · no dead air between turns 03 Live psychometric profiling Alongside the score for each answer, the interview keeps track of how the candidate is holding up, and turns that into a suggestion: press further, offer reassurance, or change the level of difficulty. Reading the answer alongside the behaviour also catches what a camera alone would miss. Few flags, each worth reading 06 Organic voice, interruptible conversation A candidate who feels they are talking to a robot performs like one, and the whole reading is worth less for it. The interviewer acknowledges answers as they come and gives way when somebody speaks over it, so people relax into it and show you how they actually communicate. Because the three are read together as the candidate speaks, it can follow up, clarify or encourage at the pace of a real interview. What is the single-pass design, and why does it change interview quality? + It settles the assessment, the read on the candidate and the next question together rather than one after another. Designs that take them in sequence leave a long silence between turns, and a silence changes how people behave: they fill it, or they tighten up. Keeping the cadence conversational is the condition the whole reading assumes. How does it stop candidates using AI assistance during a remote interview? + In two ways. During the interview it watches for the signs that somebody is being helped and raises them only when it is confident, so a phone on the desk is not a flag and reading from one is. It also compares what is being said with how it is being said: an answer that is word perfect while everything else says the candidate is uncomfortable is a contradiction no single reading would catch, and the session is marked for someone on your team to review. Does it need an internet connection? + No. BehaviourLens AI is built to run entirely inside your own environment, including networks with no internet access at all. Everything it needs to hold the interview and produce the report is installed with it, which is why it is used for clearance and other sensitive hiring. How does it know what to ask? + From the material you give it before the interview: the job description, the candidate's résumé and any answers you expect. Questions are built from what the role requires and what the candidate says they have done, and the next one is prepared while the current answer is still being given, which is what removes the pause other systems leave between turns. What is the scoring methodology? + Every answer is assessed against what the role actually asks for, and the session is read for consistency, for whether the candidate improved or tired as it went on, and for how steadily they handled pressure. Those come together as one score and a tiered recommendation (Strong Hire, Hire, Consider, Reject), and the report shows what sits behind each part of it. Can it adapt its questioning to how the candidate is doing? + Yes. After each answer it chooses what serves the interview best: move on when the answer was good, probe when it was thin, ask again when it was unclear, offer encouragement when the candidate is struggling, or close the session. There is a limit on how long it can stay with one topic, so nobody is questioned in circles. What happens to the video and audio afterwards? + The video is not kept. Camera images are read while the interview is running and are never saved, so what remains is the assessment and the evidence behind it. Audio is encrypted while it is held and deleted on the schedule you set, each customer's data is stored separately, and every session is recorded in a way that lets a decision be checked and attributed later. Recording Analysis Findings Report Frequently Asked Questions Does DeepAudioGuard detect AI generated voices? − DeepAudioGuard is designed to examine recordings for signs associated with AI generated, cloned, or manipulated voices. It considers multiple characteristics of the recording and presents the findings as an understandable authenticity assessment. Can DeepAudioGuard work without an internet connection? + Certain deployment configurations can perform the core audio authenticity analysis within a controlled local environment without relying on external analysis services. Some optional capabilities may require connectivity depending on how the product is configured. This distinction is also stated in the product documentation. What types of recordings can be analysed? + The documented workflow currently supports compatible WAV audio and MP4 video files. When video is submitted, the voice content is prepared for audio authenticity analysis. Can DeepAudioGuard determine whether a recording is legally admissible? + DeepAudioGuard provides analytical findings and a forensic report that may support an investigation. Legal admissibility depends on the jurisdiction, evidence handling procedures, chain of custody, and other applicable requirements. The product should therefore be used as an analytical aid rather than as a replacement for qualified forensic or legal assessment. Does DeepAudioGuard require specialized hardware? + Deployment requirements depend on the expected workload and performance needs. The product can support different computing environments, with more capable infrastructure providing faster analysis where required. How is DeepAudioGuard different from a basic AI voice detector? + DeepAudioGuard is designed as an audio authenticity investigation solution rather than only a simple real or fake checker. It combines multiple findings, provides visibility into the analysis, supports flexible deployment options, and produces forensic information that can assist further review. These are the core differentiators emphasized by both the documentation and the live product page. Can an AI voice detector ever be completely certain? + No audio deepfake detector should be treated as infallible. Factors such as compression, background noise, recording quality, and rerecording can affect the available evidence. For important decisions, DeepAudioGuard findings should therefore form part of a wider investigation rather than being treated as absolute proof. What problem does DeepFakeFinder solve? + It reduces the manual effort required to search for and investigate suspected deepfake videos, bringing online discovery, identity-focused verification, deepfake analysis, case management, and ongoing monitoring into a single workflow. Does DeepFakeFinder create deepfakes? + No. DeepFakeFinder is designed for deepfake detection, synthetic media investigation, media verification, and threat monitoring. It does not create deepfake content. Is human verification still important? + Yes. AI can help identify and prioritize suspicious media, but context and investigation judgment remain important. Aadhaar One field re-set in the wrong font The submitted Aadhaar is flagged, and the check names the tell rather than only returning a score: one field has been re-typed in a font that does not match the rest of the card, and that mismatch is what marks the document as edited. Your browser does not support HTML5 video. PAN card Three edits on one PAN card Three alterations marked on a single card before it is even submitted: the name line, and two runs of the PAN alphanumeric sequence, each boxed where the check found it. The marked-up image is what goes forward for analysis. Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Cheque The MICR line and the signature The specialised system that handles cheques and alternative documents returns forgery detected. Two places carry the marks: the MICR line along the bottom edge, and the signature above it. Your browser does not support HTML5 video. Invoice Not one alteration, but several weak points The invoice comes back at high fraud risk, and the reading is cumulative rather than a single tell: digital markers left by how the file was produced, structural inconsistencies inside the document, and individual line items flagged where the check found them. What it is Image, document & identity verification DeepFraudGuard helps organizations determine whether photographs, documents and identity records appear real, manipulated or artificially generated. It brings different forms of digital evidence together to identify suspicious alterations and present the findings in a clear, understandable way. Users can submit files directly through the platform or connect verification with existing business workflows. The result is a straightforward authenticity assessment supported by visual findings and plain language explanations, helping teams investigate suspicious media and documents with greater clarity. Because a forgery has to fool all of them together, none slips through on a single weak check. The appropriate verification process is selected according to the submitted content. Can DeepFraudGuard detect manipulated documents? + Yes. Supporting visual findings help reviewers identify areas that deserve closer investigation. What is Fraud ID Guard? + Fraud ID Guard is DeepFraudGuard's dedicated capability for verifying supported identity documents, with Aadhaar and PAN currently supported as Indian identity documents. It is intended for situations such as onboarding and document review where organizations need greater confidence in submitted identity records. Does DeepFraudGuard only provide a fraud score? + No. The product is designed to provide an authenticity assessment together with visual findings and understandable reasoning so reviewers can see why a submitted file may require further investigation. Can DeepFraudGuard identify where a document may have been altered? + The document verification capability can highlight suspicious areas within submitted content, helping reviewers focus on regions where potential manipulation has been identified. Can it be integrated into an existing application? + Yes. DeepFraudGuard supports direct use through its web experience as well as integration with organizational systems, allowing authenticity verification to become part of existing onboarding, fraud review or investigation workflows. How does DeepFraudGuard help reduce false fraud alerts? + Rather than treating one isolated irregularity as definitive proof of fraud, DeepFraudGuard considers supporting findings together before presenting stronger conclusions. This gives reviewers more context when assessing genuine and suspicious content. Should a DeepFraudGuard result be treated as absolute proof? + DeepFraudGuard should support investigation and informed decision making rather than replace appropriate human, forensic, compliance or legal review in high stakes situations. The product's own design emphasizes evidence and explainable findings, which are valuable precisely because a reviewer can examine the basis of the assessment. Image Verification Evidence Decision Frequently Asked Questions How does DeepImageGuard know whether an image is real or fake? − DeepImageGuard examines every image in several independent ways at the same time instead of relying on one method. Each check looks for a different sign that an image has been edited or created by AI, and the findings are brought together into a single clear result of real or fake with a confidence level. Because the checks are independent, an image has to look convincing to all of them, not just to one. Will DeepImageGuard wrongly flag my real images? + Protecting real images is built into how the result is decided. A result is only treated as highly confident when at least two independent checks point the same way, so one uncertain reading is never enough on its own. Every result also arrives with visual evidence and an explanation in everyday language, so your team can see what was actually found rather than trusting a number. What image formats does DeepImageGuard support? + The formats most organisations already work with are supported, including JPG, PNG, WEBP, GIF, BMP, TIFF, AVIF and HEIC. You can upload images through the secure web application or send them from systems you already use. Can DeepImageGuard be connected to our existing systems? + Yes. Alongside the web application, DeepImageGuard can be connected to the applications and workflows your teams already use, so image checks happen as part of normal work rather than as a separate task. Each organisation is given its own secure access with a daily usage allowance that can be set to match the volume you expect. Does image detection accuracy improve over time? + Yes. Difficult cases are reviewed by specialists and used to refine the service as new kinds of image manipulation appear, with careful checks before any change takes effect. Administrators oversee that process, while everyday users can flag any result they believe deserves a second look. How is DeepImageGuard different from DeepFraudGuard? + DeepImageGuard focuses on image authenticity alone: whether a photograph is genuine, edited or created by AI. DeepFraudGuard is the broader product that also covers document checks and identity document verification. If images are the only thing you need to verify, DeepImageGuard is the focused choice. Architecture DeepVideoGuard runs as a set of independent services. A secure interface handles video submission, dedicated workers run the authenticity checks, and a protected store keeps the evidence for each analysis. Processing Every submitted video joins a managed queue and is analysed in the background. Users follow the progress as it runs, and request limits keep large volumes of video moving in an orderly way. Security Access is granted on a verified basis only. Accounts are confirmed by email, passwords are never stored in readable form, and media and reports reach only the authenticated owner. Video Verification Evidence Decision Frequently Asked Questions What does DeepVideoGuard check in a video? − DeepVideoGuard checks whether a video is authentic or shows signs of AI generated, altered or manipulated content. It examines several signals at once, including visual appearance, movement, facial behaviour, sound and the consistency between what is seen and what is heard. Because many independent checks run on the same footage, manipulated video has to pass all of them rather than only one. The findings are then brought together into a single authenticity assessment that is easy to read and act on. What do I receive after an analysis? + Every completed analysis returns two things: a structured forensic report and an annotated diagnostic video in high definition. The report summarizes the authenticity assessment together with the supporting findings, in a form that is easy to review, share and keep on file. The annotated video shows where in the footage closer review may be required, rather than leaving you with a result alone. Between them, a reviewer can understand not only the outcome but the reasons behind it. Can the results be used as evidence? + Yes. The forensic report is prepared for evidence and documentation workflows, and it carries an integrity value so it can be confirmed later as unaltered. It records the authenticity assessment alongside the supporting findings, so a reader can follow how the result was reached. Organizations use it for investigations, audit trails, compliance records and legal review, including law enforcement and the courts. How do I submit a video, and can it handle large volumes? + Videos can be submitted securely through the web platform or through the API, so verification fits either a manual review process or an existing system. Each submission is placed in a managed queue and analysed in the background, and you can follow the progress of the check as it runs. Because the work is queued and processed automatically, large or sudden volumes of video stay orderly. That makes the platform suitable for teams that verify video regularly rather than occasionally. How is my video kept secure? + Access is granted on a verified basis only. Accounts are confirmed through email verification, passwords are never stored in readable form, and every session is checked before any video, report or result is released. Uploaded footage and finished reports are delivered only to the authenticated owner of the analysis. The platform is also hardened against attempts to reach content that belongs to another account. FacePay proves a live, enrolled person is at the handset and is willingly approving this payment: five behavioural signals fused on-device in two to three seconds, before the transaction clears. Request a demo Book a walkthrough What it checks before authorising A live person, not a photo or a replay The enrolled identity, not a lookalike Behavioural congruence across the signals Genuine consent, not coercion Output A Trust Factor: proceed, block, or escalate On-device analysis, from the moment of approval to the authorisation decision 2–3s On-device analysis, from the moment of approval to the authorisation decision Behavioural signals fused: face, micro-expression, gaze, posture and voice 5 Behavioural signals fused: face, micro-expression, gaze, posture and voice Passwords, PINs or OTPs required at the moment of payment 0 Passwords, PINs or OTPs required at the moment of payment One-time enrolment: every payment after it is validated by behaviour 1 One-time enrolment: every payment after it is validated by behaviour The moment of approval One payment, end to end Static biometrics answer whose face this is. The harder question is whether that person meant to approve this particular transaction, or was made to, which is a question about the seconds around the approval, not about the face 01 Capture Front camera and mic sample the moment of approval, on-device 02 Fuse Five behavioural signals scored together rather than in sequence 03 Score A Trust Factor for this transaction, not for this device 04 Decide Proceed, block, or escalate to secondary verification 05 Challenge High-value or anomalous: a head nod or spoken confirmation All five stages execute inside the secure enclave. No frames, no audio and no behavioural profile leave the handset: the payment app receives a decision, never a face. How it ships Embedded, enrolled once, then invisible FacePay is not a separate app a customer has to be talked into. It is an SDK the payment app already embeds, and after a single enrolment the customer never thinks about it again. The embedded component Lightweight, embedded by the payment app itself Enables FacePay as either an optional or the default authentication method. No change to the underlying UPI, NEFT, RTGS or wallet rails. Secure enclave execution On-device, with hardware acceleration The whole analysis completes in two to three seconds. Frames, audio and the behavioural profile never leave the handset. There is no central biometric store, and so nothing central to breach. One-time enrolment A single secure capture of face and behaviour Builds the profile once, on the customer's own device. Every payment after that is validated against it: no password, no OTP. Step-up challenge Triggered on high-value or anomalous transactions A head nod or a spoken confirmation, layered on top of the passive check. Raises the bar exactly where the exposure sits, rather than on every payment. Enrolment is the only moment a customer is asked to do anything unusual. Everything after it happens inside a payment they were making anyway. The architecture Five signals in, one decision out, and none of it leaves the handset The cards above are how FacePay ships. This is where the line sits. Face Micro-expression Gaze Posture Voice Fused, not sequenced On-device fusion What it checks before authorising A live person, not a photo or a replay The enrolled identity, not a lookalike Behavioural congruence across the signals Genuine consent, not coercion Secure enclave · the handset No frames, no audio and no behavioural profile leave the handset. There is no central biometric store, and so nothing central to breach. The payment app receives a decision, never a face Trust Factor Proceed The transaction clears Escalate Secondary verification Block The transaction is stopped The behavioural layer Four signals that a static biometric cannot see Facial recognition confirms the enrolled identity. These four confirm that the person behind it is live, present and acting freely, and each has its own page on the platform. Micro-expression Facial Emotion Recognition Fleeting emotional cues that read as stress or coercion rather than a routine payment. Ocular dynamics Eye Tracking Analysis Blink pattern and gaze direction: liveness, and whether attention is on the transaction. Body position Posture & Behaviour Body language carrying duress, or anomalous against how this customer normally pays. Voice Speech Sentiment Emotional state and intent in the spoken confirmation, where one is asked for. The full eight-model engine Why traditional authentication fails Credentials prove knowledge, not intent PINs, passwords and static biometrics all answer a question that fraudsters stopped needing to defeat. The gap they leave is the one sophisticated fraud now operates in. A password proves a secret was known It can be phished, socially engineered, or lifted by malware. None of that establishes that a person is at the handset at all. A face match proves identity, not consent It confirms whose face it is. It cannot tell you whether they meant to approve this payment, or were standing next to someone who made them. Coercion has a signature Micro-expression, gaze and posture read duress. That protects the customers most often targeted (elderly and less confident users) better than any credential can. Fewer chargebacks, not only fewer frauds Intent verified at the moment of approval removes the dispute as well as the loss, which is the half of the cost most fraud tooling leaves behind. Nothing central to steal The behavioural profile stays inside the secure enclave. There is no template database to breach, which is the failure mode of every centralised biometric scheme. Adaptive, not a fixed rule The engine keeps learning new fraud patterns as they appear. A PIN policy does not. Use cases by sector Where fragmented information hides the bigger picture Fraud investigation Examine whether apparently separate names, accounts, profiles or associated organisations may belong to the same wider identity or network, before moving into deeper fraud analysis. Banking and financial services Identity context across authorised sources when reviewing suspicious applications, connected parties or unusual account activity, complementing established KYC, AML and fraud controls rather than replacing them. How the sector deploys it Law enforcement and investigations Organise incomplete clues: a name in one case, a social profile in another, an organisation in a third, into a more connected investigation view. How the sector deploys it Corporate investigations Structure scattered information in authorised cases involving impersonation, misconduct, conflicts of interest or suspicious external relationships. How the sector deploys it Trust and safety Investigate possible connections between profiles and digital identities that appear unrelated when viewed individually, and understand coordinated or repeated activity. How the sector deploys it Due diligence and compliance Establish whether records found across different sources refer to the same underlying person or organisation, while preserving the need for human verification. OSINT investigations A focused identity resolution layer for open source work that produces large numbers of disconnected results. Deployment strategy Introduce identity intelligence without losing control of sensitive information 01 Define the investigation scope Identify the types of identity investigations the organisation needs to support and the sources that may lawfully be used. Clear boundaries improve both relevance and governance. 02 Establish authorised access Define which investigators, analysts and administrators may use the platform and what information they are permitted to review. Identity intelligence should never become unrestricted organisational search. 03 Connect approved information sources Introduce only the sources that fit the investigation purpose, legal basis and data governance requirements. Others can be considered as operational needs evolve. 04 Apply governance controls Set policies for access, investigation records, retention, review and deletion before operational use, particularly where identifiable personal information is involved. 05 Validate investigation workflows Begin with controlled investigations to confirm how identity findings should be interpreted and reviewed within existing processes. 06 Expand according to need Once the workflow is validated, extend into wider OSINT, fraud, compliance or security investigation environments where appropriate. 01 · Define the investigation scope Interface simulation: an illustration of the workflow, not a live analysis What it has to get right Accuracy, context, privacy and human judgement Four things identity intelligence has to get right. Identity is more than a matching name Names, usernames and other identifiers overlap. Reliable identity intelligence examines the wider context before suggesting that two records belong to the same person or organisation: connected evidence rather than one field alone. A connection needs an explanation Analysts should be able to understand why two identity records appear related, so useful context is presented alongside a potential relationship instead of an unexplained result. Personal information needs protection Identity intelligence involves sensitive personal information. Organisations need control over who can investigate, what information can be used and how long findings are retained, with privacy and governance in place from the beginning. AI should assist, not accuse Automated analysis can highlight patterns a person would take much longer to find. It should not decide that someone is fraudulent, criminal or responsible for an activity: consequential conclusions stay with authorised professionals. Clue Discovery Comparison Case Frequently Asked Questions What is Identity Intelligence Engine? − A cross platform identity resolution and linkage solution that helps authorised investigation teams connect fragmented identity information, so analysts can see whether records found in different places may relate to the same person, profile or organisation. What does identity resolution mean? + Determining whether different pieces of information may refer to the same underlying identity. Where an investigator finds several records or profiles that look related but carry different information, the platform organises and compares those signals for review. Is this a people search engine? + Not in the traditional sense. A people search focuses on finding records; this focuses on understanding the relationships between identity information already available to an authorised investigation. Can it connect information from different platforms? + Yes. Cross platform identity linkage is a core purpose. Where suitable and authorised information is available, records appearing across different sources can be examined for connected identities. Does every suggested connection mean it is the same person? + No. A surfaced relationship is investigation intelligence that requires context and review. Similar information does not prove that two records belong to the same individual. Does the system make decisions automatically? + No. It identifies and organises possible relationships, but significant conclusions should be reviewed by an authorised person. Does it access private information? + It should be configured around information the organisation is lawfully authorised to access. It is not a mechanism for bypassing privacy controls or obtaining restricted information. How is it different from SocialIntel Analyzer? + SocialIntel Analyzer investigates publicly visible social media activity across supported platforms. Identity Intelligence Engine focuses on identity resolution and cross source linkage. They are complementary within a broader OSINT environment. How is it different from AML Intelligence? + This resolves identities and their relationships; AML Intelligence is for financial crime and transaction pattern analysis. Keeping them separate keeps each purpose clear while identity context can support authorised downstream investigations. Can it help with synthetic identity investigations? + Identity linkage gives useful context where investigators are examining fragmented or inconsistent identity information. Specialised synthetic identity fraud detection should still be treated separately: not every identity mismatch indicates fraud. Does it replace KYC or identity verification? + No. It provides identity correlation and investigation context. Formal verification, KYC, regulatory screening and authentication should continue to use the organisation's dedicated processes and controls. Can it be deployed in a controlled environment? + Yes. Identity investigations involve sensitive information, so controlled organisational deployment is part of the design. Specific arrangements follow the organisation's security, privacy and operational requirements. content.text: SyntheticFraudGuard AI | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Products / Syntheticfraudguard Ai Zero-Trust Identity SyntheticFraud Guard AI Graph analytics to detect synthetic identities. Request a demo See all products Synthetic fraud, which blends stolen and fake identity data into fictitious personas, is harder to detect than traditional fraud and exploits legitimate systems to build credibility. With cases rising worldwide, it is projected to surpass $3 trillion by 2026, making it one of the gravest financial crime threats. AI-driven synthetic fraud is eroding trust in financial systems by bypassing traditional verification. Institutions must adopt dynamic, AI-powered defenses to preserve credibility, as global fraud losses hit $485.6 billion in 2023, with synthetic fraud emerging as a major driver due to its scale and sophistication. Countries Most Affected United States: The global epicenter, with synthetic identities being used to open bank accounts, secure loans, and launder money. India: Experiencing a rise in impersonation fraud through gaming, UPI transactions, and digital lending platforms. European Union: Facing coordinated attacks exploiting cross-border regulations, especially in remittances and credit issuance. Southeast Asia & Africa: Growing fintech adoption without mature regulatory oversight makes them prime targets for fraudsters. A report says, Synthetic identity fraud is noted as a growing concern, with losses in the U.S. alone projected to reach $23 billion by 2030. Juniper Research forecasts global fraud losses for financial institutions to rise from $23 billion in 2025 to $58.3 billion by 2030, driven largely by synthetic identity fraud, which uses a mix of real, stolen, and fake information to create fraudulent personas. Another source, the ACFE Insights Blog, mentions Interpol's estimate of $3 trillion in annual global cyberfraud profits. (Global synthetic fraud losses are projected to surge from $485.6B in 2023 to $3T by 2026. Financial institution fraud alone is expected to hit $58.3B by 2030) Impact Across Industries: Banking: Synthetic identities bypass KYC and AML checks, causing billions in credit and loan defaults. Impersonation Scams: Criminals exploit deepfakes and spoofing for account takeovers and mule accounts. Gaming & Virtual Platforms: Synthetic accounts drive money laundering, illegal betting, and in-game financial fraud. E-commerce & Payments: Fraudsters use synthetic IDs for large-scale account creation and purchase fraud. The Scale of the Threat According to industry forecasts, global synthetic fraud losses are expected to surpass $3 trillion by 2026 , threatening trust in financial systems and digital platforms alike. Solutions from FaceOff AI ( FO AI) Directly targets fictitious personas by orchestrating continuous behavioral biometrics (e.g., gaze, micromotions, device hygiene). It monitors for "build-up" patterns (like gradual credit building) using LSTM for temporal inconsistency detection, preventing strikes before they occur. Tips to Spot & Mitigate Synthetic Fraud 1. Look for inconsistencies in documents (mismatched SSN, Aadhaar, or phone details). 2. Monitor behavioral biometrics to spot unusual user interactions. 3. Deploy deepfake detection to prevent impersonation during digital onboarding. 4. Use federated learning models for cross-bank fraud intelligence without compromising data privacy. 5. Educate users on scams exploiting deepfakes, gaming impersonation, and digital lending traps. Synthetic fraud often builds "sleeper" identities over time, exploiting gaps in static checks. FaceOff's orchestration counters this by monitoring dynamic, hard-to-fake cues, detecting inconsistencies that reveal fabrication. Core Orchestration Framework: Adaptive Cognito Engine (ACE) FaceOff (FO AI) tackles synthetic fraud by leveraging its Adaptive Cognito Engine (ACE) as the central orchestrator. ACE fuses eight core AI models with Agentic RAG, Federated Learning, and synthetic fraud detection modules to integrate multimodal data, enable real-time analysis, ensure continuous authentication, and deliver adaptive trust scoring. ACE acts as FaceOff’s “brain,” orchestrating multimodal inputs across onboarding, KYC, and transactions. Powered by Agentic AI and RAG, it cross-validates signals to prevent siloed detection, reducing false positives by 20–40% in high-risk cases like digital lending and UPI payments. Key orchestration principles: # Modular Integration: 8 core models feed ACE; Agentic RAG adds reasoning with threat intelligence. # Federated Learning: Decentralized model training ensures privacy (DPDP/GDPR) while spotting cross-border fraud. # Real-Time Scalability: API-first, cloud/edge ready, delivers results in 2–3 seconds. # Explainable Outputs: Trust score (1–10) with clear breakdowns for risk-based decisions. Synthetic fraud is no longer a niche threat. It is a systemic global risk . Combating it requires advanced behavioral biometrics, liveness detection, AI-powered trust systems, and global collaboration across regulators, banks, and digital ecosystems. Without decisive action, financial crime will continue to escalate, undermining digital trust. Overall, FaceOff's orchestration transforms fraud detection from reactive to proactive, leveraging AI's strengths against its own misuse in synthetic fraud. By fusing dynamic signals and collaborative learning, it restores trust in digital ecosystems amid projections of $3T global losses by 2026. content.text: Telecom & Handset OEMs | Solutions | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Solutions / Alliance With Mobile Phone Companies Financial Services Telecom & Handset OEMs Verification that runs on the handset itself, helping carriers protect against SIM swap, support safer activation, and identify fraud signals during sign up Request a demo All industries Overview The handset is where trust is won or lost Verification that runs on the handset itself, helping carriers protect against SIM swap, support safer activation, and identify fraud signals during sign up A carrier decides who a customer is when a service is activated, and that decision is trusted every time the phone is used afterwards. Banks, government services and payment apps all lean on it, usually by sending a code to the number and treating whoever receives it as the customer. That inheritance is the weakness. When a number moves to another device, whether through a swap arranged at a counter or a port that should never have been approved, the trust moves with it, and every service downstream keeps honouring a decision that is no longer true. The checks below run on the device and confirm the person through their behaviour and appearance rather than relying only on a code that can be redirected, so the account stays attached to the customer rather than to whichever handset currently holds the number. What you deploy Products for Telecom & Handset OEMs These are the FaceOff products most often deployed in this sector, in the order they usually land. BehaviorBioAuth (Onboarding) Behavioral biometric identity verification Explore Facepay AI facial authentication for secure, frictionless payments Explore DeepFakeFinder Find and verify suspected deepfakes of a person across online platforms Explore Key capabilities What FaceOff checks in telecom & handset oems What this sector asks for most often, each one running at the moment a decision is being made and returning a result a reviewer can explain to somebody else Confirm a real person at activation Before a connection or a new service is activated, the applicant is confirmed as a live person rather than a photograph, a recording or somebody standing in for them, at the point where the activation can still be refused rather than after it has been used. Keep trust with the person, not the number A one time code belongs to whichever device currently holds the number. Confidence is held against the customer instead, so a number that has moved to another handset does not automatically carry the account and everything attached to it along with it. Keep checking after the session has started A session that was genuine at sign in can change hands part way through, which is where a plan change, a port request or a beneficiary edit tends to happen. The customer is confirmed quietly while the session is open, so a takeover is caught while it is running. Approve a payment at the handset A payment is approved by confirming that a live, enrolled person is present and willing, so the approval belongs to the customer rather than to a device or a code that can be redirected. It covers the everyday rails customers already use, including UPI, NEFT and RTGS. Along the foot, where the result goes once somebody has it Every decision a bank or an insurer makes about a customer rests on one question: is this person who they say they are? The diagram above opens on the left with the four ways that question actually reaches you — an application assembled from identity records, a live authorisation call, a recorded claim interview, and the photographs and video attached to a claim. Nobody in the room has met the person on the other side of any of them. The question has become harder to answer honestly. A face on a video call, a voice on a phone line and a photograph attached to a claim can all now be produced convincingly enough that looking harder does not settle it. Identity records can be assembled from real details belonging to different people, so an application passes every check it is given while the customer never existed. All four routes meet the same place in the middle, and the products named under it are the ones banks and insurers actually deploy — each has a page on this site that describes it in the same words. Running them through one engine is what stops a bank holding four separate answers, in four formats, to what is every time the same question. What comes back is on the right: whether a voice was spoken or generated, whether an image or a recording was edited or made, and the findings behind either. Along the foot is where that answer then goes — analysis you can run inside your own environment, evidence attached to every result, a reviewer who can act on it, and an audit trail a regulator, an auditor or a court can read. It is judged on whether it can show what was found, what that was based on and who decided what happened next. FaceOff runs the same checks across the sectors a government touches and keeps the reasoning with every result, so a decision is still explainable long after it was taken Request a demo All industries Overview Catching it is half the job. Being able to show it is the other half Detection that produces evidence a public body can show an auditor, with a record of what was found and what it was based on Courts, banks, hospitals and police forces all face a version of the same problem: media that may have been generated, people who may not be who they claim, and decisions somebody will ask about later. Each sector tends to buy its own answer, which is understandable, and leaves an organisation holding several tools that describe the same world in different words. For a public body the second problem is the harder one. An outcome on its own is not enough. An auditor, a public accounts committee, a tribunal or a court will ask what was found, what it was based on, who was told and what was decided, and an answer that cannot be produced on request tends to be treated as an answer that never existed. The checks below run across those sectors and report the same way, keeping the reasoning with the result and a record of what was examined. What an organisation ends up holding is not only detection, but an account of it that survives being asked about. Why does reporting the same way across sectors matter? + Because a risk function that reads one kind of finding can compare what is happening across the organisation, while one holding several tools that describe things differently spends its time translating between them. Consistency is what makes an overview possible at all. Does material have to be pooled in one place? + No. Analysis can run inside your own environment, so applying a common standard does not require gathering sensitive material from different departments into a single system first. The standard travels rather than the material. Findings return in a form those processes can already carry. What happens to sensitive material during a check? + Analysis can run inside your own environment where material is sensitive or must stay in the country, so meeting a standard does not mean handing citizens' material to somebody else in order to protect it. Can a result be wrong? + Yes. Any method of detection can be mistaken in either direction, human judgement included, so a finding is an evidence based reason to look rather than a conclusion. Common questions Insurance Fraud, answered Can it tell whether a claim photograph was edited? − Yes. DeepImageGuard checks a submitted image for signs of editing or AI generation and highlights the areas that look manipulated, so an assessor can see what was found rather than rely only on a score. Does it work on recorded claimant video? + Yes. DeepVideoGuard checks recorded video for face swaps and generated footage, and points to the specific moments that need review rather than asking someone to watch the whole file. Does it decide the claim? + No. It returns a graded finding with the evidence behind it. The decision on the claim stays with your assessors, following your own process. When in the claim does this run? + On the material as it is submitted, which means a finding is available while the claim is still open and before it is settled. That is the only point at which it can change the outcome; a check that arrives after payment has been made is a record of a loss rather than a way of preventing one. What about a photograph that is genuine but recycled from an older claim? + These checks answer whether an image was generated or altered, not whether it has been submitted before, so an unedited photograph reused from an earlier claim is not what they are looking for. Duplicate submissions are a question for your claims system. Where the same people and details keep recurring across claims that ought to be unrelated, SyntheticFraudGuard AI reads those records as connections and surfaces the group. Our claim files are forwarded and compressed before we ever see them. Does that matter? + Compressing, resizing and forwarding a file are all normal in claims handling and are not in themselves signs of tampering. What comes back is what was found in the file that was given, together with the areas or moments behind it, so an assessor can weigh a finding on a heavily forwarded image differently from the same finding on an original. Does it replace the fraud rules we already run? + No. It sits alongside them and answers a question they were not built for, which is whether the photograph, the video and the person in front of you are genuine rather than whether a claim looks unusual against your historical patterns. Findings come back in a form your existing assessment, case and audit processes can carry without a new workflow. What happens to the claim material we submit for checking? + Analysis can run inside your own environment where claim material is sensitive or must stay in the country, so checking a claim does not require handing the photographs and recordings of your customers to somebody else in order to protect them. Can a result be wrong? + Any method of detection can be mistaken in either direction, human judgement included, so a finding is an evidence based assessment rather than a guarantee. FaceOff runs where the material already is, lets each site work on its own, and leaves a record of every decision that can still be reviewed long afterwards Request a demo All industries Overview Many sites, one standard, no single pile of data Run checks across many sites and departments without pooling sensitive material in one place, and keep a record of every decision Scale changes this problem rather than simply enlarging it. A group with offices, plants, campuses or branches in many places needs the same question answered the same way in all of them, and the usual route to that is to send everything to one central system and decide there. That route creates a second problem. Pooling video, recordings and identity material turns many modest targets into one very attractive one, moves sensitive material between departments and borders that may not be permitted to share it, and leaves every site depending on a link staying up. In many organisations the rules governing the material simply do not allow it. The checks below run where the material already is. Each site works on its own and keeps its own record, so what the organisation gains is a common standard and a reviewable trail, rather than one place where everything sensitive was collected for the sake of convenience. content.text: Law Enforcement | Solutions | FaceOff Technologies Skip to content India USA Global Free online demo Become A Partner Platform Products Solutions Regulations Resources Company Sign in Request a demo Search Open menu Home / Solutions / Law Enforcement Government & Public Safety From the first recording to the courtroom An investigation now runs on material that may have been produced by software: a voice on a call, a video from a phone, an account that looks like a person with a history. FaceOff checks voice, video and online identity and returns graded findings with the reasoning attached, so an investigator can act on them now and still explain them later Request a demo All industries Overview The recording used to be the fixed point Verify identity on live camera networks, search recorded footage, and check whether a video, a voice or an online account is genuine An investigation has always leaned on recordings. A voice on a call, footage from a camera, a photograph sent between two phones. Whatever else was disputed, the recording itself was usually the fixed point everything else got measured against. That is no longer safe to assume. A voice can be copied from a short sample, a face can be placed onto somebody else's body, and an account with years of apparent history behind it can be built in an afternoon. The damage runs in both directions: a fabricated recording can send an enquiry in the wrong direction for months, and a genuine one can be brushed aside by a suspect simply claiming a machine made it. The checks below examine the material an investigation actually collects and return a graded finding with the reasoning behind it, showing what was noticed and where. That is what lets a line of enquiry be justified at the time and the work be reviewed later by a supervisor, an expert instructed by the defence, or a court. Check video before a case is built on it Video collected during an investigation is examined for face swaps and generated footage, and the finding points to the moments that need review. A long recording becomes a short list of passages worth an investigator's time rather than a day of playback. Find where else a fake of a person appears When somebody is impersonated, whether a suspect, a witness or an officer, the material rarely stays in one place. Suspected fakes of a named person are traced across online platforms and each match is checked against the real person, with the monitoring held as a case file rather than a folder of screenshots. Turn scattered public information into a case view Public information about the accounts and people involved is drawn into one structured view, including profiles that were built rather than grown and accounts that move together. An investigator starts from a picture of the case instead of assembling one by hand. Draw together records that may be one person Identity records held across different authorised sources can be resolved and linked, with the relationships laid out for an analyst to review. An identity assembled from pieces of several real people becomes visible as a group rather than passing as a set of unrelated individuals. Match a face on a camera network, with an officer deciding Faces on live cameras are matched against watch lists your own investigators build, and every match arrives graded for an officer to accept or reject. It runs on hardware you own inside your own network, and every action taken is recorded. It is written to be reviewed and challenged rather than accepted, because a conclusion an investigator cannot explain will not survive a supervisor, let alone a court. Can it tell whether a voice on a recording was cloned? + DeepAudioGuard checks recorded audio for speech that was generated, cloned or altered rather than spoken, and keeps the passages that raised concern so they can be listened to. The result is graded rather than a bare yes or no. Is a finding admissible in court? + Admissibility is decided by the court, under the rules of evidence that apply where the case is heard, and no supplier can promise it in advance. What is provided is a finding with its reasoning attached and a record of what was examined, which is what a supervisor, an expert instructed by the defence or a court needs in order to review the work. Does the software decide who becomes a suspect? + No. A camera match arrives as a graded alert an officer accepts or rejects, and every finding reaches a person with the reasoning attached. What gets recorded and acted on is the officer's decision, not the system's. Does case material have to leave our network? + CrossCam PersonTrack runs on your own hardware and makes no call outside your network in normal running, and analysis can run inside your own environment where case material is sensitive or must stay in the country. Is there a record of what was done during an investigation? + Yes. Actions are recorded and can be searched, which is what allows a line of enquiry to be reconstructed months later and what shows that a decision was taken by an officer rather than by a system. How does it help when a witness or an officer is being impersonated? + DeepFakeFinder traces suspected fakes of a named person across online platforms, verifies each match against the real person and holds the monitoring as a case file. That turns a single report into a picture of how far the material has spread, and gives the team something to take to a platform. Can it work with the recordings an investigation actually collects? + The checks are meant for recordings as they arrive rather than clean studio material. Where audio is difficult, VoiceExtract AI separates speakers and removes background noise and interference, so a recording that was going to be set aside can become usable. Can a result be wrong? + Yes. Any method of detection can be mistaken in either direction, human judgement included, and in an investigation both kinds of error land on real people. A finding is a reason to look rather than a conclusion, which is why the reasoning travels with it and why every decision stays with an officer. See it score a real video Bring your own footage. FaceOff checks the image and the identity behind it before a document is issued, and hands an examiner the findings rather than a verdict Request a demo All industries Overview A document issued once is trusted for years Check whether a facial photograph submitted with an application has been edited or generated, and whether the identity information behind it is consistent Almost everything an issuing authority does rests on a photograph and a set of details that the applicant provided. An examiner works from what was sent in, usually without ever meeting the person, and at a volume that leaves very little time for any single file. Both halves of that are now straightforward to manufacture. A facial photograph can be generated or quietly altered so that it survives a visual check while belonging to nobody at all, and an identity can be assembled from genuine details taken from several different people, so every individual detail verifies correctly while the person described has never existed. The consequence outlasts the decision by years. A passport or a visa issued on a false basis becomes a genuine document, accepted everywhere, and used to obtain everything else. The checks below examine what was submitted and give an examiner the findings behind the result at the only point where refusing is still an option. Damage that was never there, and images generated to support a story, can be caught at assessment rather than found during a later review. Law enforcement and investigations Establish whether a recording can be relied on as evidence, and record why. Findings are returned in a form an investigator can put in a case file and a colleague can follow later. Media and journalism Verify a photograph, a clip or a voice recording before it is published. A newsroom can check material from an unknown source against the clock rather than taking it on trust. Enterprise and executive protection Guard against impersonation of senior people, whose voices and faces are widely available. Suspected attempts can be assessed and kept as a record for legal follow up. Government and public sector Check submitted photographs, documents and recordings where the decision that follows is difficult to reverse. Sensitive material can be examined inside your own environment where it must not leave a jurisdiction. FAQ What people ask about SyntheticMediaGuard Answered the way a reviewer, a fraud team or a compliance lead asks them. What is SyntheticMediaGuard? − SyntheticMediaGuard is FaceOff's suite for establishing whether digital media is genuine. It examines images, video, voice recordings, live virtual meetings and the media people encounter online, and reports whether the content appears authentic or shows signs of being altered or generated by AI. It is used by organisations that have to act on media they did not create, such as banks verifying a customer, investigators assessing evidence, and teams deciding whether a call or a document can be relied on. Every product in the suite returns its result in the same form. What kinds of media can it check? + SyntheticMediaGuard checks images, video, voice and audio recordings, live virtual meetings, and media encountered while browsing. Photographs and video can be checked as files after the fact or as they arrive, voice recordings can be checked for cloned and synthetic speech, and a video call can be checked while it is still in progress. The suite can also search online platforms for material impersonating a specific person, which matters when the concern is not one file but everything circulating about someone. How does SyntheticMediaGuard explain its results? + Every completed check returns a clear assessment together with the findings that support it, so a reviewer can see why media was judged genuine, questionable or manipulated. Where the media is long, the assessment indicates which parts warrant closer review rather than leaving a single verdict over the whole file. The result is written to be read by the person making the decision, not only by a specialist, and it is prepared in a form suitable for investigations, compliance reviews and audit records. Can it detect a deepfake during a live video call? + Yes. Virtual meetings can be checked while they are running, on the platforms organisations already use, so a swapped face or a synthetic participant can be flagged during the conversation rather than discovered afterwards. This matters most where a call itself authorises something such as a payment instruction, an approval or an identity check, because by the time a recording is reviewed the decision has usually already been made. What happens to the media and biometric information it examines? + SyntheticMediaGuard is designed to assess media without building a store of the biometric detail it examines, so verifying whether media is genuine does not leave an organisation holding a new collection of faces and voices. Analysis can also be run within an organisation's own environment where the material is sensitive or must not leave a jurisdiction. The intent is that a media authenticity check reduces risk overall rather than trading one exposure for another. Who uses SyntheticMediaGuard? + SyntheticMediaGuard is used by banks and financial services teams verifying customers and payment instructions, insurers assessing claim photographs and video, law enforcement and investigation teams weighing recordings as evidence, newsrooms verifying material before publication, and enterprise security teams protecting senior people from impersonation. What these teams have in common is that they have to make a decision on media somebody else produced. Is a result ever wrong? + SyntheticMediaGuard produces an evidence based assessment of risk, not a guarantee. Synthetic media techniques change continuously, and any method of detection, including human judgement, can be mistaken in either direction. That is precisely why every result is returned with the findings behind it. The assessment is there to inform the person deciding, to focus attention on what deserves scrutiny, and to be examined and challenged rather than accepted without question. It watches for accounts impersonating your people and brand, and it establishes whether records held in different places describe the same person, so an investigator starts with a picture rather than a pile of tabs. Scattered open sources · linked by edge · resolved to one Open sources · one person Social profile Marketplace listing Company record News mention Forum post Payment alias Domain registration Resolved to One person A red edge is a link the graph is asserting, and it is shown with what supports it The information needed to understand a person or an incident is usually available already. The difficulty is that it sits in many places, none of which talk to each other, and an analyst spends most of their time gathering it rather than thinking about it. TrustShield OSINT does the gathering. It watches public channels for accounts impersonating your executives or your brand, and for activity that looks coordinated rather than genuine. Separately, it works out whether records held across the sources you are entitled to use describe one person or several, and shows how they connect. What comes back is a starting point rather than a verdict. Connections are presented with the reasons they were drawn, so an analyst can follow them, discard the ones that do not hold, and record what they concluded. The work of judging is left where it belongs.
